```md
# Ecosystem merge plan

How the sibling projects fold into SlopStation, what landed, and
what was deliberately left out.

Scope rule: everything merged here is for **hardware you own** — homebrew
payloads, your own debug builds, your own dumps. Anything whose purpose is
cheating in live online games, evading bans, or circumventing licensing is
not merged and will not be extended.

## Landed in this repo

| From | What landed | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ps4debug-mcp | UDP broadcast discovery (`target.ps4_discover`, `host:"auto"`) | `src/core/mcp/tools_target.cpp`, `kBroadcastMagic/kBroadcastPort` in `src/core/runtime/ps4_protocol.hpp` |
| ps4debug-mcp | JSONL audit log on every MCP tool call (`mcp_audit_enabled`, `mcp_audit_path` settings) | `call_tool` wrapper in `src/core/mcp/mcp_tools.cpp` |
| ps4debug-mcp | `confirm:true` gate for mutating actions (`mcp_require_confirm` setting) | same wrapper; mutating set in `action_mutating()` |
| afterglow-web | `host` MCP tool: HTTP payload host with index page, `/files/<name>`, auto `/manifest.json` (sha256 per file), token required on non-loopback binds, `put` action | `src/core/mcp/tools_host.cpp` |
| ps4-injection-lab | Homebrew injection recipe book (userland methods only) | `docs/injection/README.md` |
| ps4debug-NG | Already the wire transport; fork extensions exposed as `ps4_*` actions | `src/core/runtime/backend_ps4.cpp` |
| PS4-MCP | Session broker (`broker_gate`, client registry) + GDB Remote Serial bridge (full RSP: threads, regs, memory, breakpoints/watchpoints, async stop replies) so the UI, MCP agents and a GDB client share one console connection | `src/core/runtime/broker.*`, `src/core/runtime/gdb_rsp.*`, `gdb` tool in `src/core/mcp/tools_gdb.cpp` |
| PS4-MCP | IDA/Ghidra/Binary Ninja/iaito analyzer adapters, rewired to the built-in MCP server via a `BrokerClient` shim (MCP JSON-RPC instead of the Rust broker `/rpc`) | `integrations/ps4-mcp-adapters/` |

## Still external (by design)

- **ps4debug-mcp** (Python client/CLI) stays a standalone companion client;
  its safety model is now also enforced server-side in this repo, so agents
  get the same guarantees through the built-in MCP server.
- **PS4-MCP** (Rust rmcp server) is fully absorbed for dev tooling: broker +
  GDB-RSP bridge in `src/core/runtime`, analyzer adapters in
  `integrations/ps4-mcp-adapters/`. Its game-project authoring (`games.rs`)
  stays out per the scope rule above.

## Explicitly not merged

- Apex/Fortnite PS4 cheat payloads and per-game cheat offsets (live online
  games; harms other players).
- HWID spoofing, kernel/DMA/Bluetooth-spoof injection methods, GoldHEN
  cheat XML — anti-cheat evasion and ban evasion.
- License-key generation / auth bypass and customer loaders.

If you want any of those, that's a hard no — not a configuration toggle.

## Settings added

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mcp_audit_enabled` | `true` | append every MCP tool call to the audit log |
| `mcp_audit_path` | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\reverse-slop\mcp_audit.jsonl` | audit log location; empty disables |
| `mcp_require_confirm` | `false` | mutating console/target actions need `"confirm": true` |
| `host_token` | empty | bearer token required for non-loopback `host.start` binds |

`docs/api/README.md`:

```md
# MCP and HTTP endpoints

The engine's listener binds `127.0.0.1` only.

| Endpoint | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /health` | Liveness and version |
| `POST /mcp` | MCP JSON-RPC 2.0: `initialize`, `ping`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/list`, `resources/read`, `prompts/list`, `prompts/get` (protocol `2025-06-18`) |
| `GET /mcp` | MCP SSE endpoint: keepalive plus `notifications/progress` for a `tools/call` that carried `_meta.progressToken` |
| `POST /api/v1` | Direct frontend RPC; one request or an array |
| `POST /api` | Deprecated alias of `/api/v1` (answers with a `Deprecation` header) |
| `GET /api/v1/events` | Frontend SSE stream: `hello`, `output`, `boot.stage`, `target.changed`, `backend.changed`, `hype.progress`, `watch.list`, `watch.values`, `debugger.stop`, `debugger.state`, `debugger.log`, `types.changed`, `disasm.index_updated`, `app.quitting` |
| `GET /events` | Deprecated alias of `/api/v1/events` |
| `GET /api/v1/openapi.json` | OpenAPI 3.1 descriptor generated from the MCP tool schemas |

`initialize` also returns `instructions` (a usage preamble) and `state` (backend badge,
attached target, debugger state, loaded image, analysis readiness). The same context is
available through `target.status` and `disasm.loaded`.

## Examples

```powershell
Invoke-RestMethod http://127.0.0.1:8765/health

$body = @{ tool = 'target'; action = 'ps4_auto'; params = @{ host = '192.168.1.50' } } | ConvertTo-Json
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://127.0.0.1:8765/api/v1 -ContentType 'application/json' -Body $body

$body = @{ jsonrpc = '2.0'; id = 1; method = 'tools/call'
           params = @{ name = 'target'; arguments = @{ action = 'list' } } } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 8
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp -ContentType 'application/json' -Body $body
```

Every request needs the bearer token unless the endpoint says otherwise:

```powershell
$h = @{ Authorization = "Bearer $env:SLOP_MCP_TOKEN" }
Invoke-RestMethod -Headers $h http://127.0.0.1:8765/health
```

## Response shape

`/api/v1` answers `{ "ok": true, "data": … }`; a tool failure is
`{ "ok": false, "data": { "error": "…", "hint": "…" } }` (the hint is added when the engine
knows a better call). A request body that is an array is answered with an array of the same
envelopes, so opening a view costs one round trip. `/mcp` answers plain JSON-RPC:
`result.content[0].text` carries the JSON payload, and tool failures come back as
`isError: true` with the same object.

## Event stream

`/api/v1/events` authenticates with a single-use ticket from `app.events_ticket` (60 s
TTL) — no token in URLs. Events are `text/event-stream` frames named after the list above;
`watch.values` carries the sampled watchlist at about 10 Hz, and `hello` opens the stream.
Concurrent streams are capped by the `events_max_streams` setting (default 64).

## OpenAPI

`GET /api/v1/openapi.json` returns an OpenAPI 3.1 document generated from the same tool
schemas `tools/list` serves, so a generated client and an MCP agent never disagree about
parameters.

## Resources

`resources/list` exposes the live state and every guide playbook as a resource:

| URI | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `slop://state/target` | active backend, attached target (pid, name, arch), busy flag |
| `slop://state/image` | shared binary session: path, format, arch, analysis state |
| `slop://guide/<topic>` | the playbook JSON for one `guide` topic |

`resources/read {uri}` returns `contents[0].text` with the JSON body; an unknown URI is an
error.

## Prompts

`prompts/list` returns one prompt per guide topic (name, title, summary, no arguments), and
`prompts/get {name}` returns that playbook as a single user message, so an MCP client can
offer the workflows as slash commands.

## Guides

`guide.list` and `guide.get {topic}` return ready-to-run tool sequences:
`ps4_setup`, `ps4_breakpoint`, `ps4_api_trace`, `ps4_find_write`, `ps4_step_trace`,
`ps4_remote_call`, `find_health`, `find_damage_source`, `pointer_chain` and more. They are
the fastest way to learn the intended call order for a task.

```

`docs/api/clients.md`:

```md
# MCP client registration

On the first successful start on the configured port, a `slopstation` HTTP entry is added
(existing entries are kept) to:

| Client | File |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `%USERPROFILE%\.claude.json` (user scope, `"type": "http"`) |
| Cursor | `%USERPROFILE%\.cursor\mcp.json` |
| Windsurf | `%USERPROFILE%\.codeium\windsurf\mcp_config.json` |
| VS Code | `%APPDATA%\Code\User\settings.json` (`mcp.servers`) |
| OpenCode | `%USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode\config.json` |

Unparseable config files are left untouched. When a token is set, it is written into these
files — **do not sync them publicly**. Run the engine with `--no-onboard` to skip
registration; set `mcp_onboarded` to `false` to request another pass.

## Stdio-only clients

Claude Desktop and friends run the engine with `--stdio`: JSON-RPC arrives on stdin and
leaves on stdout one message per line, logs go to stderr, and a per-process token is
generated automatically. If an engine is already running (the desktop app), the stdio
process bridges to it instead of starting a second one.

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "slopstation": {
    "command": "C:\\Users\\you\\AppData\\Local\\dev.slopstation.ui\\engine\\reverse-slop-engine.exe",
    "args": ["--stdio"] } } }
```

## Manual HTTP entry

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "slopstation": {
    "type": "http",
    "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp",
    "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <token>" } } } }
```

The token is in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\reverse-slop\settings.json` (`mcp_token`), or in the
`SLOP_ENGINE_READY <port> <token>` line the engine prints on start when it is run as a
sidecar.

## Live checks in the repo

`tools/mcp_stdio_test.py` drives a stdio session, `tools/mcp_live_test.py` drives the HTTP
endpoint of a running app. Both are dependency-free Python and are what CI uses to prove
the wire protocol still works.

```

# Configuration and security

{
  "mcp_enabled": true,

  "web_allow_private": false,
  "mcp_onboard_clients": [],
  "mcp_token_in_configs": false,
  "mcp_rate_limits": {},
  "events_max_streams": 64,
  "proxy_redact_secrets": true,
  "fs_root": []
}
```

| Key | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mcp_enabled` | bool | start the MCP/HTTP listener (default `true`) |
| `mcp_port` | int 1–65535 | listener port (default 8765) |
| `mcp_token` | string | bearer token; **not settable** through `app.settings_set`, use `app.rotate_token` |
| `mcp_onboarded` | bool | set `false` to request another client-registration pass |
| `mcp_onboard_clients` | array of strings | clients to register (empty = Tern when installed, else every known client) |
| `mcp_token_in_configs` | bool | write the literal bearer into client configs instead of `${SLOP_MCP_TOKEN}` (default `false`) |
| `mcp_rate_limits` | object | per-tool token buckets `{tool: {rate, burst}}`; tools without an entry use the built-in defaults |
| `mcp_require_confirm` | bool | mutating actions need `"confirm": true` |
| `mcp_audit_enabled` | bool | write the JSONL audit log (default `true`) |
| `mcp_audit_path` | string | where the audit log goes (default `%LOCALAPPDATA%\reverse-slop\mcp_audit.jsonl`) |
| `events_max_streams` | int 1–1024 | concurrent `/api/v1/events` streams (default 64) |
| `script_unsafe` | bool | full Lua standard library (`io`/`os`) |
| `web_allow_private` | bool | allow loopback/LAN targets in `web.fetch`/`web.post` |
| `web_allowlist` | array of strings | hosts reachable when private targets are allowed |
| `proxy_token` | string | token for the localhost inspection proxy |
| `proxy_redact_secrets` | bool | redact secret headers and query values in stored proxy entries (default `true`) |
| `fs_root` | string or array of strings | jail every `fs` action to these folders; unset keeps the historic whole-profile access |

`app.settings_get` returns the settings with `mcp_token`/`proxy_token` redacted to
`"set"`/`"unset"`; `app.settings_set {key, value}` validates the typed keys above and
erases a key when `value` is `null`.

## Rate limits

`mcp_rate_limits` is a per-tool token bucket, consulted on `/mcp` only (`/api/v1` never
throttles the UI). An entry is `{"rate": <tokens per second, > 0>, "burst": <>= 1>}`; a
malformed entry means no limit for that tool rather than a wrong one. Tools without an
entry use the built-in defaults:

| Tool | rate | burst |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `memory` | 50 | 100 |
| `emulate` | 20 | 40 |
| `xray` | 30 | 60 |
| `analyze` | 10 | 20 |
| `devirt` | 20 | 40 |
| `script` | 20 | 40 |

## Filesystem jail

`fs_root` is unset by default, which keeps the historic whole-profile access. Set it to one
path or a list of paths and every `fs` action is confined to them: paths are canonicalised
first, so `..`, junctions, 8.3 names, `\\?\` prefixes and alternate data streams cannot
walk out, and directory walks never follow reparse points. The engine data directory is
refused either way.

## Tokens

- **A bearer token is generated automatically on first start**; every `/mcp` and `/api/v1`
  call needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Regenerate it from Settings
  (`app.rotate_token`) — client configs and `engine.json` are updated in place.
  `SLOP_MCP_TOKEN` adds a per-process token without persisting anything.
- `SLOP_MCP_PORT` or `--port` overrides the port. If the port is busy the engine takes an
  ephemeral port and skips onboarding.
- The event stream (`/api/v1/events`) authenticates with a **single-use ticket** from
  `app.events_ticket` (60 s TTL) — no token in URLs.

## Request hardening

- Request bodies are capped at 32 MiB.
- Every route validates `Host` and browser `Origin` (DNS-rebinding and cross-site
  JSON-RPC get 403).
- The listener binds `127.0.0.1` only.
- The audit log records every tool call, allowed or refused, with secrets redacted.

## What is dangerous

Treat `script.run` as code execution regardless of the sandbox — the `slop.*` surface
writes memory and files. Live writes and `ps4_*` mutating actions are code execution
against the target: a bad write can crash the console or the game. Read
[`SECURITY.md`](https://github.com/NetVar1337/SlopStation/blob/main/SECURITY.md) and the
[audit](../AUDIT.md) before running untrusted payloads or scripts.

```

## Action hints

`tools/list` carries a description per tool and per action. The engine also returns a
`hint` on failure when it knows the right next call — for example a PE-only action on an
ELF image points at `target.ps4_dump_module`, and `ps4_*` on a local session points at the
composite flows that do work locally.

## Mutating actions

Writes, patches, scans that allocate on the console, payload sends and `script.run` are
classified as mutating. With `mcp_require_confirm` on they need `"confirm": true`, and
every call — allowed or refused — is written to the JSONL audit log with secrets redacted.

`docs/benchmarks/README.md`:

```md
# Benchmarks

Recorded performance baselines for the app-side hot paths, and the tooling that
checks them.

| File | Produced by | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| `app-before.json` / `app-after.json` | `build\tests\slop_app_bench.exe <out.json>` (`src/tests/bench_app.cpp`) | Memory scanner, traffic-store slicing, event bus and MCP `output`/`diag` paths: median of 7 runs per workload plus allocation volume and a deterministic `result` per workload. |
| `ui-before.json` / `ui-after.json` | `npm run bench -- <out.json>` in `app/` (`app/scripts/bench-ui.mjs`) | Server-side render of the Output panel with 4096 rows, plus a 1,000,000-row virtualized list mounted in jsdom (mount, scroll frame, filter). Component work only, not browser frame time. |

`*-before.json` / `*-after.json` are the pair recorded around the optimization
that introduced them; **`*-after.json` is the current baseline**. `ui-before.json`
predates the `virtual_list_1m_rows` workload, so only `ui-after.json` carries it.

## 1M-row virtualized list

`virtual_list_1m_rows` mounts `app/src/bench/VirtualListBench.tsx` — 1,000,000
synthetic rows, no engine — in jsdom, warms the render path with 10 scrolls,
then records:

| Metric | Baseline | Budget |
|---|---|---|
| `mount_ms` | 77.9 | generic 3x |
| `scroll_frame_ms` | 4.43 | **1.25x** |
| `filter_ms` | 383.7 | generic 3x |

`scroll_frame_ms` is the tenth percentile of 60 scroll-and-render frames (the
median is kept as `scroll_median_ms`): the fastest frames still carry the real
render cost, while a busy machine only inflates the rest. It is the hot path of
the listing, so the weekly bench lane fails when it regresses more than 25%
against `ui-after.json`; the other two keep the generic slowdown factor.

## Checking for regressions

```powershell
powershell -NoProfile -File tools\run_benchmarks.ps1            # build, run, compare
powershell -NoProfile -File tools\run_benchmarks.ps1 -SkipBuild  # reuse build\tests\slop_app_bench.exe
```

The script fails when a workload's `result` changes (a correctness change) or its
median exceeds `-MaxSlowdown` (default 3x) times the baseline. The factor is
generous on purpose: the baselines come from a developer machine and CI runners
are slower and noisier, so only real regressions trip it. The one exception is
the 1M-row list's `scroll_frame_ms`, which fails past 1.25x (see above).

CI runs the same script weekly and on demand (`.github/workflows/bench.yml`),
writes a comparison table to the run summary, and uploads the raw JSON.

## Comparing two runs

```powershell
powershell -NoProfile -File tools\compare_app_bench.ps1 -Baseline docs\benchmarks\app-before.json -Candidate build\bench\app.json
```

prints per-workload speedup and allocation deltas (and fails if a workload's
result differs).

## Updating the baseline

After an intended performance change, on a quiet machine:

```powershell
powershell -NoProfile -File tools\run_benchmarks.ps1 -UpdateBaseline
```

copies the run over `app-after.json` / `ui-after.json`; commit them together
with the change.

```

`docs/encrypted-self.md`:

```md
# Encrypted PS4 SELF images

A retail PS4 `eboot.bin` (and most `.sprx`) is a **SELF**: a 0x20-byte header,
a table of 0x20-byte segment entries, then the embedded ELF header and program
headers. Each loadable program header's bytes live in a *blocked* SELF segment
(`flags & 0x800`) whose id (`flags >> 20`) is the program header index.

Retail builds flag those segments **encrypted** (`flags & 0x2`) and signed
(`flags & 0x4`). The decryption keys live in the console's secure module and
never leave it, so an encrypted SELF cannot be decrypted offline — not by this
tool, not by any host-side tool.

## What the engine does

`disasm.load` / `disasm.load_self` parse the SELF segment table before
touching the ELF. When any blocked segment carries the encrypted flag the load
fails immediately with an actionable error naming the segment, its program
header index, its file offset and its stored size, for example:

```
encrypted SELF: 3 of 5 data segments are encrypted (first: SELF segment 1 =
program header 1 at file offset 0x2000, 4096 bytes stored). Retail
eboot.bin/.sprx files are decrypted only on the console; ... call
target.ps4_dump_module {name, load:true} ... and load that file instead
```

Fake-signed / unencrypted SELFs (homebrew, devkit builds, and dumps that were
re-signed) load normally: the loader rebuilds a plain ELF from the segments,
inflating deflated ones.

## Getting a decrypted image

The decrypted bytes exist **in the console's memory** once the title is
running. Two supported sources:

### 1. Dump from live memory (recommended)

Requires a PS4/PS5 in a jailbreakable firmware running ps4debug-NG (or a
compatible payload) with the game launched.

```
target.ps4_connect  { "host": "192.168.1.50" }
target.ps4_auto     { "host": "192.168.1.50" }      # connect + attach
target.ps4_modules                                   # find eboot.bin's base
target.ps4_dump_module {
  "name": "eboot.bin",
  "path": "C:/dumps/eboot.bin",
  "load": true                                       # rebuild ELF + load it
}
```

`target.ps4_dump_module` reads the module's whole mapped range over the wire
and, with `load: true`, rebuilds an ELF64 with one `PT_LOAD` per console
segment at its runtime VA. The result loads straight into the disassembler with
addresses matching the live console, so breakpoints and static VAs agree.
`complete: false` in the reply means some pages were unreadable and were
zero-filled; re-dump after the title finishes loading if that matters.

### 2. Extract from an fpkg

An fpkg (`*.pkg`) built with a decrypted `eboot.bin` — or any tool that
produces the plain ELF (e.g. a homebrew dumper, or `pkg` tooling that decrypts
with console-side keys) — gives you a file you can load directly:

```
disasm.load_self {
  "path": "C:/games/CUSA00000/eboot.bin",   # the original SELF, for reference
  "decrypted_dump": "C:/dumps/eboot.elf"    # the decrypted image to analyze
}
```

or simply `disasm.load { "path": "C:/dumps/eboot.elf", "relocate": false }`
for a memory dump (dumps already carry the loader's relocations; pass
`relocate: false` so the engine does not apply them twice).

## Why not decrypt here

The SELF encryption is AES with per-title keys derived inside the console's
secure processor. The host never sees them. Any "decrypt" option in a PC tool
is either (a) operating on a fake-signed image that was never encrypted, or
(b) bundled console keys, which this project does not ship. The error path and
`docs/encrypted-self.md` exist so the workflow is explicit instead of silently
producing noise from ciphertext.

## Limits

- `disasm.load_self` inspects the SELF header/segment table only; the analysis
  always runs on the decrypted image.
- A memory dump's VAs match the console's runtime base. Keep the dump's base
  when loading (`base` omitted or the console base) so annotations and
  breakpoints line up.
- Encrypted `.sprx` modules follow the same flow: dump the module by name with
  `target.ps4_dump_module`.

```

`docs/features/console-connection.md`:

```md
# Console connection (ps4debug-NG)

SlopStation speaks the [ps4debug-NG](https://github.com/Pharaoh2k/ps4debug-NG) wire
protocol directly: commands on TCP 744, debug events on TCP 755.

- `target.ps4_connect {host, port=744, pid?}`, `ps4_disconnect`, `ps4_reconnect`,
  `ps4_auto`, `ps4_discover` (UDP broadcast), `ps4_dump_module`, `ps4_send_payload`.
- Reads are validated against the console VM map, so unmapped ranges fail instead of
  returning zeros. Windows `PAGE_*` constants are translated to FreeBSD `VM_PROT_*`.
- The port-755 listener accepts only the attached console and drains each connection on
  its own thread.
- Reconnect keeps the session usable: the engine resets debug and turbo-scan sessions,
  restores breakpoint slots where the payload allows it, and says so in the error text
  when a connection generation changed mid-call.

## Discovery

`ps4_discover` broadcasts the 4-byte magic `0xFFFFAAAA` to `255.255.255.255:1010` and
collects every payload that answers with the same magic (the ps4debug-mcp convention).
`host: "auto"` on `ps4_connect`/`ps4_auto`/`ps4_send_payload` runs the same probe and uses
the first answer.

## Bundled payload

The installer and the app carry the ps4debug-NG payload (GPLv3). The build always fetches
the **latest release**:

- `tools/fetch_ps4debug.ps1` queries `releases/latest`, downloads the `.bin` asset and
  writes `build/ps4debug-ng/manifest.json` (tag, asset, URL, SHA-256, fetch time) plus the
  GPLv3 license text.
- The manifest and payload are bundled under `payloads/ps4debug-ng/`.
- The **Targets → ps4debug-NG payload** card shows the bundled/local tag, checks the latest
  release and downloads a newer payload to
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\dev.slopstation.ui\payloads\ps4debug-ng\`.
- **Send to console** streams the payload to the console's BinLoader over one fresh TCP
  connection (port 9090); **Save payload…** exports the `.bin` for FTP or a GoldHEN
  payload loader. The engine action is `target.ps4_send_payload {host, port, path?}`.

ps4debug-NG is a separate GPLv3 program, not linked into the MIT-licensed SlopStation code;
its source is at <https://github.com/Pharaoh2k/ps4debug-NG>.

## Payload host

`host.start {port, bind, token}` serves a directory over HTTP with an index page,
`/files/<name>` and an auto-generated `/manifest.json` carrying a sha256 per file. A token
is required on non-loopback binds. `host.put` uploads a file. This is how you serve your
own payloads to the console without a separate web server.

## GDB bridge

`gdb.start` (loopback only, `allow_writes` opt-in) exposes the console session over the GDB
Remote Serial Protocol so IDA, Ghidra, Binary Ninja or iaito can attach through the same
connection the UI and MCP use. See
[`integrations/ps4-mcp-adapters/`](https://github.com/NetVar1337/SlopStation/tree/main/integrations).

## Walkthrough

[First console connect](../tutorials/first-console-connect.md) covers the whole path with
the failure modes.

`docs/features/decompiler.md`:

```md
# Decompiler

The `decomp` tool lifts code through the vendored Hyperion engine: p-code lifting, SSA,
dead-code elimination, type inference and structuring to C-like output. Calling conventions
supported are SysV AMD64, Win64 and AAPCS64.

```json
{ "tool": "decomp", "action": "function", "params": { "addr": "0x140001000" } }
```

`decomp.function` is the only action. It waits up to 10 s for the background analysis, then
returns the pseudocode. Failure modes are explicit:

| Reply | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `no image loaded in reverse-slop` | load a binary first (`disasm.load`) |
| `hyperion engine unavailable for this image` | the format has no Hyperion backend |
| `hyperion analysis in progress` | still running — poll `disasm.loaded` → `hype.ready` |
| `hyperion analysis not running, <error>` | it failed or was cancelled; re-run `disasm.load` |

Related calls that read the same database:

```json
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "blocks", "params": { "addr": "0x140001000" } }
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "globals", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "vtables", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "xray", "action": "cff", "params": {} }
```

From Lua: `slop.decomp.decompile(va)`, `blocks(va)`, `vtables()`, `globals()`, `rtti()`.

## Reading the output

- Names come from the analyzer (`functions[].name`) unless you renamed the address with
  `disasm.symbol_set`; user names win.
- Types come from inference, so structs are reconstructions. Declare your own with the
  `types` tool (`create_struct`, `add_member`, `read_field`, `format_at`) and they persist
  per image.
- Control-flow flattening shows up as a `while` over a state variable; `xray.cff` scores it
  and `patch.resolve_opaque` can clean up the predicates.

```

`docs/features/emulation-devirt.md`:

```md
# Emulation and devirtualization

## Emulator

`emulate.run` executes x86-64 in an isolated Unicorn instance:

- start from raw bytes, a loaded-image address, or a live target address;
- demand paging from the loaded image or live memory, so untouched pages cost nothing;
- IAT stubs that log calls;
- custom registers, stack and memory;
- stop conditions, bounded traces and byte-granular taint.

```json
{ "tool": "emulate", "action": "run",
  "params": { "file_addr": "0x140001000", "code_len": 256, "count": 200, "trace": true } }
```

The code source is `hex`, `file_addr` (an address in the loaded image) or `target_addr`
(live memory, with `code_len`); `entry` overrides the start address, `count` caps
instructions, `until` stops at an address, and `page_in` (default true) faults pages in from
the image or the target on demand. `arch` accepts `x64`/`x86_64`/`amd64` or
`arm64`/`aarch64`, and `orbis_syscalls:true` services PS4 syscalls.

### Slices from a recorded trace

```json
{ "tool": "emulate", "action": "slice",
  "params": { "trace_id": 1, "reg": "rax", "at": "0x140001020" } }
```

`run` with `trace:true` returns a `trace_id` (the last eight traces stay addressable).
`slice` walks that trace backwards from `at` (or from the instruction that last wrote
`reg`, or from `addr`) and returns the instructions that produced the value.

### Persistent sessions

```json
{ "tool": "emulate", "action": "session_create",
  "params": { "file_addr": "0x140001000", "count": 0 } }
{ "tool": "emulate", "action": "session_run", "params": { "session": 1, "count": 500 } }
{ "tool": "emulate", "action": "session_step", "params": { "session": 1 } }
{ "tool": "emulate", "action": "snapshot", "params": { "session": 1 } }
{ "tool": "emulate", "action": "restore", "params": { "session": 1 } }
{ "tool": "emulate", "action": "session_destroy", "params": { "session": 1 } }
```

A session keeps the VM between calls: `session_step` runs one instruction, `session_run`
runs `count` (0 = until a stop condition, 5 s default budget), and every reply carries the
register state. `snapshot` checkpoints the pages written so far and `restore` returns to the
newest checkpoint; up to eight sessions are live at once.

## Devirtualization

The `devirt` tool covers VM-based protectors:

| Action | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `identify` | recognize the VM and its entry points |
| `handlers`, `opcode_map` | handler discovery and the opcode → handler map |
| `trace`, `lift`, `pseudocode` | run the VM, lift handlers, emit pseudocode |
| `recover_cfg` | rebuild the control-flow graph behind the VM |
| `prove_predicates`, `invariants` | prove opaque predicates, list invariants |
| `iat_audit` | audit the import table for redirected entries |

## Magicmida (Themida)

Supervised Magicmida jobs with architecture checks, cancellation and timeouts:

```json
{ "tool": "devirt", "action": "themida_status", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "devirt", "action": "themida_start",
  "params": { "path": "C:/samples/packed.exe", "output_path": "C:/samples/unpacked.exe" } }
{ "tool": "devirt", "action": "themida_job", "params": { "id": 1 } }
{ "tool": "devirt", "action": "themida_cancel", "params": { "id": 1 } }
```

The sidecars are fetched by `tools/install_magicmida.ps1` and cached in CI; the ImGui shell
has a dedicated **Unpacker** view for this, the Tauri app drives it through MCP
(see the [parity matrix](../imgui-shell.md#feature-parity)).

`docs/features/live-debugging.md`:

```md
# Live debugging

The `debugger` tool drives the console's ps4debug debugger, and the same tool carries the
`ps5_*` subset for ps5debug-NG. The four one-shot composite flows also run on a local
Windows process (see [A local process, no console](../tutorials/local-process.md)).

| Group | Actions |
| --- | --- |
| Session | `ps4_attach {pid}`, `ps4_detach`, `ps4_status`, `ps4_console_info` (branding, caps, server version, fw, foreground app) |
| Breakpoints | `ps4_bp_set {addr, condition?, hits?}`, `ps4_bp_clear`, `ps4_bp_list` (slots 0–29) |
| Watchpoints | `ps4_watch_set {addr, len, type}`, `ps4_watch_clear`, `ps4_watch_list` (DR0–DR3) |
| Run control | `ps4_continue`, `ps4_step`, `ps4_suspend`/`ps4_resume`, `ps4_process_stop` |
| Events | `ps4_wait {timeout_ms}`, `ps4_events {max, clear}` |
| Registers | `ps4_regs`, `ps4_set_reg`, `ps4_dbregs`, `ps4_set_dbregs`, `ps4_fpregs`, `ps4_set_fpregs`, `ps4_fsgs`, `ps4_set_fsgs` |
| Stack | `ps4_callstack`, `ps4_stack` |
| Remote calls | `ps4_call {addr, args[6]}` — installs the payload RPC stub once per process |
| Power actions | `ps4_until`, `ps4_find_write`, `ps4_trace_calls`, `ps4_trace_steps` |
| Trace sessions | `ps4_trace_start`, `ps4_trace_status`, `ps4_trace_stop` |
| Native scan | `ps4_auth`, then `ps4_scan`, `ps4_rescan`, `ps4_scan_state`, `ps4_scan_reset`, `ps4_scan_all`, `ps4_scan_aob` |

## The basic loop

```json
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_attach", "params": { "pid": 1234 } }
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_bp_set", "params": { "addr": "0x484490" } }
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_continue", "params": { "stop": 0 } }
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_wait", "params": { "timeout_ms": 10000 } }
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_regs", "params": { "lwpid": 101 } }
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_callstack", "params": { "lwpid": 101 } }
```

Breakpoints are software INT3 slots 0–29; watchpoints are hardware DR0–DR3 with a length of
1, 2, 4 or 8 and a type of `exec`, `write` or `rdwr`. `ps4_wait` blocks for the stop event
on port 755 and returns `rip`, registers and the signal; `ps4_events` drains the queue
non-blocking.

## One-shot flows

```json
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_find_write",
  "params": { "addr": "0x200001000", "len": 4, "timeout_ms": 10000 } }
```

`ps4_find_write` arms a write watchpoint, resumes, waits for the hit and returns the event
plus the writer's callstack — the answer to "who changed this value".

| Action | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `ps4_until {addr, timeout_ms}` | `halted`, stop event, `bp_was_armed`, `skipped_stops` |
| `ps4_find_write {addr, len, timeout_ms, depth}` | `event`, `callstack`, `writer_rip` |
| `ps4_trace_calls {addr, count, timeout_ms}` | `hits[]` with `rip` and the 6 argument registers |
| `ps4_trace_steps {lwpid, count, timeout_ms}` | `steps[]` with `rip` and disassembled text |

`ps4_trace_calls` reports the argument registers in SysV order (`rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8,
r9`); a local Win64 target passes `rcx, rdx, r8, r9`. The target stays stopped at the last
hit — `ps4_continue` resumes it.

## Remote calls

```json
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_call",
  "params": { "addr": "0x8001234", "args": [1, 2, 3, 0, 0, 0] } }
```

`ps4_call` installs the payload RPC stub once per process (`CMD_PROC_INTALL`) and calls the
address with up to six arguments, returning `rax`. Use it to invoke game functions, resolve
exports via module base + offset, or run shellcode you wrote with `memory.alloc` +
`memory.write`.

## Registers and stack

`ps4_regs` returns the full general-purpose set, `ps4_fpregs` the FP/SIMD state,
`ps4_fsgs` the FS/GS bases, `ps4_dbregs` the debug registers. `ps4_callstack` walks the
`rbp` chain through live reads; `ps4_stack` dumps raw stack memory.

## Trace sessions

The one-shot flows stop at a fixed count. A trace session runs in the background and
streams records to a JSONL file instead:

```json
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_trace_start",
  "params": { "mode": "calls", "addr": "0x484490", "path": "C:/tmp/trace.jsonl",
              "ring_size": 4096, "count": 0, "timeout_ms": 5000 } }
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_trace_status", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_trace_stop", "params": {} }
```

`mode` is `steps` or `calls` (`calls` takes `addr`, `steps` takes `lwpid`); `path` is
required. Records stay in the ring buffer until `ps4_trace_stop` — or `count` — flushes them
to `path`; `ps4_trace_status` previews the newest eight and reports `records`, `buffered`,
`dropped`, `stop_reason` and `flushed`. Only one trace runs at a time.

## PS5

The `debugger` tool drives a PS5 the same way through ps5debug-NG; connect with
`target.ps5_connect {host}` (or `ps5_auto`) first. The subset is
`ps5_status`, `ps5_console_info`, `ps5_attach`, `ps5_detach`, `ps5_threads`, `ps5_app`,
`ps5_bp_set`/`ps5_bp_clear`/`ps5_bp_list`, `ps5_watch_set`/`ps5_watch_clear`/`ps5_watch_list`,
`ps5_continue`/`ps5_step`/`ps5_suspend`/`ps5_resume`, `ps5_wait`/`ps5_events`,
`ps5_regs`/`ps5_set_reg`, `ps5_notify` and `ps5_print`. There is no PS5 remote call, trace
session or native scan; `target.ps5_notify {msg}` shows an on-screen notification.

## The Debugger view

![Debugger view: registers, callstack, breakpoints, watchpoints and the event feed](../screenshots/debugger.png)

The **Debugger** tab shows the same state: a **Continue** button, a step control
(*Step one lwp (0 = all threads)*), a wait button, **Detach**, the register and callstack
columns, **Breakpoints** and **Watchpoints (DR)** lists with address/type/length inputs, the
event feed, and the dump row (**dump+load**). Before a console is attached it offers
**Attach debugger (ps4debug)**.

```

`docs/features/live-memory.md`:

```md
# Live memory

The `memory` tool works on the console session and on a local Windows process alike.

- Read/write in hex, UTF-8, integer and float formats; allocate, free, change protection.
- Initial and refined numeric scans: exact/range/changed/unchanged, signed/unsigned/float
  widths, rounding, region/protection/alignment filters, worker/chunk/result caps.
- AOB wildcard search, pointer-chain scans and verification, signature generation, live
  crypto-constant search.
- Memory snapshots with compare/list/free; `scan_save`/`scan_load` persist an address-list
  scan across restarts, and `scan_export {path}` writes the current hit set as
  `address,type,value` CSV.
- `dissect {addr, size}` classifies what each 8-byte slot of an unknown object is: pointer
  to code, object or string, float, double, integer, or text.
- `watch_export_ct {path}` / `watch_import_ct {path}` move the watchlist to and from a
  Cheat Engine `.CT` table.
- `offsets_verify`: fingerprint-gated offset manifests. A manifest pins the build (title
  ID, app version, SHA-256 of the module's executable segment) and gives every offset an
  anchor signature that must match exactly once; any mismatch returns no addresses at all.
  Format in [`src/core/memory/offsets.hpp`](https://github.com/NetVar1337/SlopStation/blob/main/src/core/memory/offsets.hpp).
- Shared watchlist sampled about 10 Hz with freeze writes; UI and MCP edits appear in
  both. `watch_freeze_once` releases after the first write-back and `watch_undo` restores
  the captured value.

## Scans

```json
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "scan",
  "params": { "kind": "exact", "width": "u32", "value": 100 } }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "rescan",
  "params": { "kind": "decreased", "width": "u32" } }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "scan_state", "params": {} }
```

Kinds: `exact`, `between`, `bigger`, `smaller`, `unknown`, `increased`, `increased_by`,
`increased_percent`, `decreased`, `decreased_by`, `changed`, `unchanged`. Widths: `i8`,
`u8`, `i16`, `u16`, `i32`, `u32`, `i64`, `u64`, `f32`, `f64`, or `all`.

Useful extras on `scan`: `begin`/`end` to bound the range, `alignment` (fastscan),
`tail` (1–8 hex digits, "ends with" fastscan), `writable`/`executable` region filters,
`max_results`, `threads`, `chunk_bytes`.

## Watchlist and freeze

```json
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "watch_add",
  "params": { "addr": "0x200001000", "width": "u32", "label": "player.health" } }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "watch_set", "params": { "id": 1, "freeze": true } }
```

`watch_add` latches the live value immediately, so a freeze has something to write back;
`freeze_armed` in the reply tells you whether it actually armed.

## AOB and pointer chains

```json
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "aob", "params": { "pattern": "48 8B ?? ?? 89" } }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "pointerscan",
  "params": { "target": "0x200001000", "depth": 5, "max_results": 32 } }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "pointerscan_verify",
  "params": { "chains": [ { "base": "0x200000000", "offsets": [16, 32] } ] } }
```

`??` matches any byte. `pointerscan` walks static roots and reads pointer chains out of
live memory, returning the address path for each hit; `pointerscan_verify` re-checks
explicit chains (or the last pointerscan of this target) against the current session.

## Snapshots and diffs

```json
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "snapshot", "params": { "label": "before" } }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "diff", "params": { "a": 1, "b": 2 } }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "snapshots", "params": {} }
```

`diff` takes two snapshot ids and returns the changed `offset`/`length` ranges;
`snapshot_free {id}` releases one, and `snapshots` lists what is held.

## Dissecting an unknown object

```json
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "dissect", "params": { "addr": "0x2004A0000", "size": 256 } }
```

`size` defaults to 256 bytes and is capped at 4096; the reply labels every 8-byte slot as a
pointer to code, object or string, a float, a double, an integer or text, so an unknown
structure can be mapped before `types.declare` describes it.

## Offsets that survive a game update

`offsets_verify` takes a manifest that pins the exact build and gives every offset an
anchor signature. If the game updated, the fingerprints or signatures stop matching and the
call returns no addresses instead of silently wrong ones.

## Walkthrough

[Find and freeze a value](../tutorials/local-process.md) — the scanner and watchlist on a
local process, and [Live debugging](live-debugging.md) for the "who writes this" flow.

`docs/features/lua.md`:

```md
# Lua scripting

Scripts run from the **Scripts** panel (`Ctrl+Enter`), the `script` MCP tool
(`action=run`, `code`, `timeout_ms`) or `/api`, against the same session as the UI —
renames and comments made in one surface show up in all of them. Returned values are
appended as `return: <value>`.

Scripts are sandboxed by default (no `io`/`os` execution, memory and instruction caps);
set `script_unsafe` in Settings for the full standard library.

```lua
-- read the player struct on the console, then rank the dump's functions
local st = slop.target.status()
print("backend:", st.backend, st.name, st.pid)
local raw = slop.mem.read_bytes(0x200001000, 12)         -- raw bytes
local hp, ammo, lives = string.unpack("<i4i4i4", raw)
print("player: hp=" .. hp .. " ammo=" .. ammo .. " lives=" .. lives)

-- the debugger surface is scriptable too
slop.ps4.attach(st.pid)
slop.ps4.bp_set(0x484490)
local ev = slop.ps4.wait(5000)
print(("stop: rip=0x%X thread=%s"):format(ev.rip, ev.thread))

local fns = slop.disasm.functions(4000)
table.sort(fns, function(a, b) return a.size > b.size end)
for i = 1, 5 do
  print(string.format("%X  %s  %d bytes", fns[i].va, fns[i].name, fns[i].size))
end
```

![Lua scripts panel](../screenshots/scripts.png)

## API surface

| Group | Functions |
| --- | --- |
| Core | `slop.version()`, `slop.log(msg)` |
| Target | `slop.target.list()`, `attach(pid)`, `status()` |
| Memory | `slop.mem.read_hex(addr, len)`, `write_hex(addr, data)`, `scan(...)` |
| Image session | `slop.image.load(path[, base])`, `load_from_target`, `unload`, `status`, `wait_ready([ms])` |
| Instructions | `slop.disasm.decode(addr[, count])`, `bytes(addr[, len])`, `disassemble(...)` |
| Functions / xrefs | `slop.disasm.functions([limit])`, `function_at(va)`, `xrefs_to(va)` |
| Data | `slop.disasm.strings([min[, limit]])`, `slop.disasm.pe()` |
| Annotation | `slop.disasm.name/set_name/comment/set_comment`, `bookmark_toggle`, `bookmarks` |
| Decompiler | `slop.decomp.decompile(va)`, `blocks(va)`, `vtables()`, `globals()`, `rtti()` |
| Analysis | `slop.analyze.packer()` |

## Limits

- `timeout_ms` defaults to 5000 and is clamped to 10..60000; the deadline and MCP
  cancellation are checked every 1000 VM instructions and inside blocking calls
  (`wait_ready`, `mem.scan`, debugger waits are cut to the remaining budget).
- The Lua heap is capped at 256 MiB; `peak_mem` reports usage.
- `print()` output is captured (capped at 4 MiB, `output_truncated=true` past it).
- Scripts never hold a tool lock, so a long script cannot wedge the UI or other agents.

## Examples in the repo

[`examples/`](https://github.com/NetVar1337/SlopStation/tree/main/examples) has runnable
scripts: `ps4_find_value.lua`, `ps4_eboot_overview.lua`, `ps4_breakpoint_trace.lua`,
`ue5_dumper.lua`.

`docs/features/network-proxy.md`:

```md
# Host network and proxy

Both features act on the **analysis PC**, not the console.

## Raw capture

Raw-socket capture (SIO_RCVALL, administrator rights) with:

- packet paging with text filters, DNS log and statistics;
- stream listing and reassembly;
- per-packet HTTP/TLS/DNS inspection;
- PCAP export.

```json
{ "tool": "network", "action": "capture_start", "params": { "filter": "tcp port 443" } }
{ "tool": "network", "action": "packets", "params": { "limit": 100 } }
{ "tool": "network", "action": "streams", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "network", "action": "export_pcap", "params": { "path": "C:/tmp/cap.pcap" } }
```

`network.status`, `capture_stop`, `dns`, `stats`, `stream_data`, `reassemble_stream`,
`connections` and `deep_inspect` complete the surface.

## Localhost inspection proxy

An independent HTTP/1.1 proxy on loopback: start/stop, captured exchanges, replay.

```json
{ "tool": "proxy", "action": "start", "params": { "port": 8080 } }
{ "tool": "proxy", "action": "entries", "params": { "limit": 50 } }
{ "tool": "proxy", "action": "replay", "params": { "id": 1 } }
```

CONNECT tunnels record metadata and SNI only. TLS interception (`mitm_enable`) requires
explicit consent, installs a local CA, and is fully reversible (`mitm_uninstall`).

## Outbound HTTP

The `web` tool does WinHTTP GET/POST without inheriting browser cookies. Private and
loopback targets are denied unless `web_allow_private` is on (and then only what
`web_allowlist` allows).

`docs/features/on-console-tooling.md`:

```md
# On-console tooling

These actions run **inside the payload** on the console, so they are fast and do not stream
memory over the network.

- **Turbo Scan & bulk writes**: `ps4_turbo_caps`, `ps4_turbo_regions`, `ps4_turbo_config`,
  `ps4_turbo_scan`, `ps4_turbo_rescan`, `ps4_turbo_results`, `ps4_turbo_cancel`,
  `ps4_turbo_end`, and `ps4_write_multi` (up to 65,535 verified writes in one round-trip).
- **Fork extensions**: `ps4_modules` (server-side module list) and `ps4_snapshot`
  (one-round-trip region stream); `target.modules` uses `CMD_PROC_MODULES` with a
  client-side fallback on upstream payloads.
- **Native scan** (unlocked by `ps4_auth`): `ps4_scan`, `ps4_rescan`, `ps4_scan_state`,
  `ps4_scan_reset`, `ps4_scan_all`, `ps4_scan_aob` (`??` wildcards).
- **Code analysis**: `ps4_disasm`, `ps4_xrefs`, `ps4_xrefs_to`.
- **Assembly**: `ps4_assemble {asm, base?, syntax?}` (payload-side Keystone).
- **ELF upload**: `ps4_elf_rpc {path}`, `ps4_elf_load {path}`.
- **Console**: `ps4_notify`, `ps4_print`, `ps4_app` (foreground pid, title ID, content ID).

## When to use which

| Situation | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Narrow a large value scan | `ps4_turbo_scan` / `ps4_turbo_rescan` (server-side) |
| Write many addresses at once | `ps4_write_multi` |
| Disassemble live console code | `ps4_disasm` (payload Zydis) |
| Find references to a live address | `ps4_xrefs`, `ps4_xrefs_to` |
| Load your own code | `ps4_elf_load` / `ps4_elf_rpc` — see [Injection recipes](../injection/README.md) |
| Tell the player something | `ps4_notify` |

All of these are mutating actions where they write: with `mcp_require_confirm` on they need
`"confirm": true`, and every call lands in the JSONL audit log.

## Turbo scan

```json
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_turbo_caps", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_turbo_scan",
  "params": { "value_type": "u32", "compare": "exact", "value": 100 } }
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_turbo_results", "params": { "limit": 100 } }
```

`ps4_turbo_caps` tells you whether the payload build supports turbo scan at all (it is a
ps4debug-NG fork extension); on an upstream payload the native `ps4_scan*` family is the
fallback, and `ps4_auth` unlocks it.

# Feature map

| Area | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| **Console connection** | ps4debug-NG over TCP 744 plus the TCP 755 debug-event callback; ps5debug-NG for PS5. UDP auto-discovery, saved consoles with quick-switch, manual reconnect (`ps4_reconnect`), native/turbo scan and bulk writes. |
| **Live memory** | Regions, modules, threads, read/write/protect/alloc, Cheat Engine-style scans, AOB wildcards, pointer chains, snapshots and diffs, object dissection, a shared watchlist with freeze/freeze-once/undo. |
| **Live debugging** | Software breakpoints (conditional, hit counts), DR0–DR3 watchpoints, continue/step/suspend, stop events with registers, callstacks, FP/FS-GS, remote calls, trace/find-write one-shots, JSONL trace sessions; the `ps5_*` subset for PS5. |
| **On-console tooling** | Native scan/rescan, Turbo Scan, verified bulk writes, fork module/snapshot commands, Zydis disassembly, xrefs, Keystone assembly, ELF upload. |
| **Static analysis** | ELF64 with NID→name resolution, SELF, PE, Mach-O/`.ipa`, .NET; function/xref/string indexes; Xray passes; patching with a journal; binary diffing; packer heuristics. |
| **Decompiler** | Hyperion p-code lifting, SSA, DCE, type inference and structuring to C-like output (SysV AMD64, Win64, AAPCS64). |
| **Emulation** | Isolated Unicorn x86-64/arm64 runs with demand paging from the loaded image or live memory, tracing, backward slices, persistent sessions with checkpoints, byte-level taint and devirtualization helpers. |
| **Automation** | Lua 5.4 against the shared session, plus an MCP server with action-based tools, task playbooks (`guide`), a JSONL audit log and an optional confirm gate. |
| **Payload host** | Built-in HTTP payload host with a sha256 `manifest.json`; UDP broadcast discovery; the bundled ps4debug-NG payload. |
| **Host network** | Raw-socket capture, DNS log, stream reassembly, PCAP export, and a localhost HTTP inspection proxy. |

Two desktop shells drive the same C++ core: the **Tauri v2 + React** app (the one that
ships) and a legacy **ImGui/DX11** shell ([documented here](../imgui-shell.md)). The
engine also runs headless for MCP/HTTP clients only.

`docs/features/persistence.md`:

```md
# Persistence, filesystem and web

## Persistence

SQLite under the app data directory:

- session snapshots (`save`, `list`, `load`, `delete`) and key/value storage
  (`kv_set`, `kv_get`);
- Hyperion `.hdb` export/import (`hype_save`, `hype_load`), so an analyzed image can be
  reopened without re-running the analysis.

```json
{ "tool": "persist", "action": "kv_set", "params": { "key": "project", "value": "demo" } }
{ "tool": "persist", "action": "list", "params": {} }
```

Renames, comments, bookmarks and declared types also persist — per file hash, so they
remap across bases and survive restarts.

## Filesystem

Host filesystem access for the agent: `read_file`, `write_file`, `list_directory`,
`create_directory`, `delete_path`, `search_files`, `grep_in_files`.

The engine's own data directory is refused, so an agent cannot corrupt the session database
or the token store through `fs`.

## Web

`web.fetch` and `web.post` are outbound WinHTTP calls that do not inherit browser cookies.
Private/loopback targets are denied unless `web_allow_private` is set, and `web_allowlist`
narrows what is reachable when it is.

```json
{ "tool": "web", "action": "fetch", "params": { "url": "https://example.com/" } }
```

```

`docs/features/static-analysis.md`:

```md
# Static analysis

The image session is shared by the UI, MCP and Lua. One binary loaded once; every surface
sees the same functions, names, comments and patches.

## Formats

- ELF64 with **NID→name resolution** (built-in database, overridable via
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\reverse-slop\nids.txt`) and relocation application.
- SELF header/segment extraction (fake-signed/unencrypted; an encrypted retail
  `eboot.bin` fails and points at `target.ps4_dump_module`).
- PE headers/imports/exports; Mach-O thin/FAT and `.ipa`; .NET metadata.
- Fast Zydis function, xref and string indexes; Capstone for ARM64.

## What the session holds

- Background Hyperion analysis (CFGs, globals, vtables, RTTI, names) and the decompiler for
  PE and Mach-O images; .NET assemblies list types, render C#, or dump IL.
- **Xray** (read-only): CFG and cyclomatic complexity, control-flow flattening and
  obfuscation scoring, string reconstruction, indirect-call recovery, anti-analysis
  patterns, hook checks, direct syscalls, API-hash resolution, entropy windows, page
  classification, crypto constants, ROP gadgets.
- **Patching** (loaded image only): junk-NOP cleanup, opaque predicates, anti-debug, XOR
  unpack, string decoding, byte writes, a patch journal with full revert, a combined pass,
  and re-indexing after edits.
- Binary-to-binary function diff, packer/protector indicators, RTTI/vtable recovery,
  dangerous-import callsites, library signatures, user structs/enums, comments and
  bookmarks. Names/comments/bookmarks persist per file hash and remap across bases.

## Loading

```json
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "load", "params": { "path": "C:/dumps/eboot.bin.elf" } }
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "loaded", "params": {} }
```

`load` takes `base` (rebase the image to a runtime base, 0 keeps its own) and `relocate`
(default true; pass `false` for memory dumps, whose bytes are already relocated). Poll
`loaded` until `image.hype.ready` before using the decompiler or the analyzer database.
`analyze_stop` cancels a background analysis cooperatively (it returns fast when the
analysis already finished), and `unload` drops the session.

`load_self {path, decrypted_dump?}` inspects a PS4 SELF: retail `eboot.bin`/`.sprx`
segments are encrypted with keys that never leave the console, so the action either loads
the decrypted dump you point it at or explains how to get one
(`target.ps4_dump_module` from live memory, or fpkg tooling).

In the app, opening a file is the same call. The **Image Browser** tab shows sections,
imports and exports.

![PE browser: sections, imports, exports](../screenshots/pe.png)

## Indexes

| Action | Returns |
| --- | --- |
| `functions {limit, offset, filter}` | `va`, `name`, `size`, CFG stats |
| `xrefs {addr, limit}` | references to an address, with the engines that found them |
| `strings {min, limit}` | string index with addresses |
| `symbols {limit}` | user renames + analyzer names, with `source` |
| `symbol_set {addr, name}` | write a user rename (empty clears) |
| `blocks {addr}` | basic blocks of a function |
| `globals`, `vtables` | analyzer databases |
| `pe`, `managed` | headers/imports/exports, .NET metadata |
| `disassemble {addr, count}`, `assemble {asm, base, syntax}` | instruction text both ways |

## Annotations and structs

`notes.set_comment`/`notes.get_comment`/`notes.comments` and
`notes.bookmark_toggle`/`notes.bookmarks` hold the analyst layer; `notes.export {path}` and
`notes.import {path, merge}` move it as `symbols/<hash>.json` between machines
(`merge` is `ours`, `theirs` or `union`). `types.declare`, `types.create_struct`,
`types.add_member`, `types.remove_struct`, `types.create_enum`/`types.remove_enum`,
`types.read_field` and `types.format_at` describe and read your own structures.

## Binary diff jobs

`analyze.diff {path_a, path_b}` runs two full Hyperion analyses synchronously and can take
a while on large binaries. `analyze.diff_start {path_a, path_b}` returns a job id instead;
poll `analyze.diff_job {id}` for `stage`/`progress` and stop it with
`analyze.diff_cancel {id}`. Up to 32 jobs are tracked.

## Patching

```json
{ "tool": "patch", "action": "write_bytes",
  "params": { "addr": "0x2004DDA48", "hex": "90 90" } }
{ "tool": "patch", "action": "journal", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "patch", "action": "revert_all", "params": {} }
```

Every change is journaled (`va`, `before`, `after`), `revert_all` restores them, and the
indexes rebuild lazily so `functions`/`xrefs`/`strings` stay correct after an edit.

## Walkthrough

[Dump, rename, decompile](../tutorials/dump-rename-decompile.md).

```

`docs/getting-started/install.md`:

```md
# Install

## Installer (recommended)

Download `SlopStation_<version>_x64-setup.exe` from
[Releases](https://github.com/NetVar1337/SlopStation/releases/latest) and run it. The
installer is per-user (`installMode: "currentUser"` in `app/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`) —
no administrator prompt — and installs the app, the engine, the bundled ps4debug-NG
payload and the optional Magicmida sidecars.

**Auto-update is on by default.** On launch the app checks the latest GitHub release,
downloads the signed installer in the background and offers **Install & restart** in the
banner. **Settings → Updates** shows the running version and a manual check. Updates are
verified against the embedded Tauri public key; the installer is Authenticode-signed when
the signing secrets are configured.

## Portable single file

`SlopStation.exe` from the release zip (`SlopStation-portable-<tag>.zip`) is
self-contained: the engine is embedded in the executable and extracted to
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\dev.slopstation.ui\engine` on first run. No installer, no sidecar folder.
The payload card can download the latest ps4debug-NG release on demand.

## Package managers

| Manager | Command | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| winget | `winget install NetVar1337.SlopStation` | user scope, NSIS installer |
| Scoop | `scoop install slopstation` | portable zip |
| Chocolatey | `choco install slopstation` | NSIS installer, silent |

The manifests live in [`packaging/`](https://github.com/NetVar1337/SlopStation/tree/main/packaging)
and are generated from a release's `SHA256SUMS` by `tools/gen_packages.ps1`; the
`packages` workflow publishes them as artifacts on every release.

## Requirements

| Needed for | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Running the app | Windows 10/11 x64, WebView2 runtime (bundled with Windows 11) |
| Console work | A PS4 on the same network running the ps4debug-NG payload |
| Building | Visual Studio 2022+ with _Desktop development with C++_, CMake ≥ 3.25, Ninja, Node.js + npm, Rust/Cargo |
| Optional | Administrator rights for host packet capture; Magicmida for Themida unpacking |

## Verify the download

Every release ships `SHA256SUMS` next to the assets:

```powershell
gh release download v0.2.3 -R NetVar1337/SlopStation -p SHA256SUMS
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 .\SlopStation_0.2.3_x64-setup.exe
```

The hash must match the line for that file. The `.sig` file next to the installer is the
Tauri updater signature, not an Authenticode signature — the app checks it, `Get-AuthenticodeSignature`
reports the code-signing certificate when the release was signed.

```

`docs/getting-started/quick-start.md`:

```md
# Quick start

1. **Launch SlopStation.** The splash waits for the engine handshake (up to 180 s, which
   covers the UAC prompt on first run).
2. **Load the payload on the PS4.** In **Targets**, the *ps4debug-NG payload* card shows
   the bundled release. **Send to console** streams the `.bin` to BinLoader (port 9090)
   over TCP; **Save payload…** writes it wherever you want for FTP or a GoldHEN loader.
   **Check latest** compares the bundled build with the newest GitHub release;
   **Download v\<tag\>** fetches a newer one. **Discover** in the connect form finds
   consoles on the LAN via UDP broadcast.
3. **Connect.** Enter the console IP (port 744) and press **Connect**, or let an agent do
   it in one call:

```json
{ "tool": "target", "action": "ps4_auto", "params": { "host": "192.168.1.50" } }
```

`ps4_auto` connects, authenticates the native scanner, picks the game process (the one
with `/app0/` modules, eboot-named preferred), attaches a session and the debug session,
and returns modules, threads and regions.

No console handy? Click **“List this PC's processes instead”** in Targets and attach to
any local process — everything except the `ps4_*` actions works. See
[A local process, no console](tutorials/local-process.md).

## The three surfaces

| Surface | What it is | Entry point |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Desktop app | Tauri v2 + React shell over the engine's HTTP/SSE API | `SlopStation.exe` |
| MCP server | Action-based tools for AI agents, JSON-RPC 2.0 | `http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp` |
| Lua | Scripts against the same session as the UI and MCP | Scripts panel, `script.run` |

All three share one session: a rename, a comment or a watchlist entry made in one shows up
in the others.

## Keyboard

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Ctrl+K` | Command palette — functions, addresses, tabs and actions |
| `Ctrl+Enter` | Run the script in the Scripts panel |

`docs/help-index.md`:

```md
# In-app help index

`tools/gen_help_index.mjs` turns this documentation into a flat JSON index that the app can
search from the command palette. It is generated, never edited by hand, and it is not
committed — a UI slice consumes it.

## Generate

```powershell
node tools/gen_help_index.mjs                       # JSON on stdout
node tools/gen_help_index.mjs --out app/public/help-index.json
node tools/gen_help_index.mjs --base /SlopStation/ --out help-index.json
```

Exit code 0 means the index was written; 1 means a documentation file could not be read
or no section was found (so CI fails instead of shipping an empty index).

## Output contract

```json
{
  "generated": "2026-11-14T09:00:00.000Z",
  "source": "docs",
  "count": 412,
  "entries": [
    {
      "title": "Live memory",
      "anchor": "live-memory",
      "section": "Live memory",
      "text": "The memory tool works on the console session and on a local Windows process alike. Read/write in hex, UTF-8, integer and float formats; ...",
      "url": "features/live-memory.html#live-memory",
      "path": "features/live-memory.md"
    }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `generated` | ISO timestamp of the run |
| `source` | always `docs` (the mdBook `src`) |
| `count` | number of entries |
| `entries[].title` | the page title for a level-1 heading, otherwise the heading text |
| `entries[].anchor` | mdBook-compatible anchor of that heading (`#` fragment without `#`) |
| `entries[].section` | the heading text as written |
| `entries[].text` | plain-text excerpt of the section, markdown stripped, whitespace collapsed, ~240 characters |
| `entries[].url` | site-relative URL: `<page>.html#<anchor>` (prefix with `--base` for a sub-path deploy) |
| `entries[].path` | source file relative to `docs/` |

Entries are emitted in `SUMMARY.md` order, so search results follow the book's reading
order. `SUMMARY.md` itself is not indexed.

## Notes for the consuming UI

- The index is static: rebuild it when the docs change (the `docs` workflow does).
- The Tauri app consumes it: `npm run help:index` (in `app/`) writes
  `src/generated/help-index.json`, which the command palette loads lazily for its **Help**
  results. `predev`/`prebuild` run it, so a fresh checkout needs no extra step.
- Anchors are generated the way mdBook generates them (lowercase, punctuation dropped,
  spaces to `-`, `-1`, `-2`… for duplicates). If a heading is renamed, the anchor changes —
  treat `url` as opaque.
- The excerpt is plain text, not HTML: render it as text, do not inject it.

```

`docs/imgui-shell.md`:

```md
# The ImGui shell

**Decision: keep it, as a documented lightweight fallback — not as a second product.**

The Tauri v2 + React app is the shell that ships: it is what the installer installs, what
the updater updates, what the screenshots show and what the e2e driver drives. The legacy
ImGui/DX11 shell (`src/app` + `src/ui`) stays in the tree because it is cheap to keep
compiling (it is part of the same CMake build and the same CI lane) and it is useful when:

- you want the workbench **without WebView2, Node or Rust** — a plain Win32 binary that
  links the same `slop_core`;
- you are debugging the core itself and want a shell with no IPC boundary;
- you need the **Magicmida unpacker UI**, which only exists there today.

It is not a supported end-user surface: no auto-update, no MCP client onboarding, no
settings UI, no Lua panel. Do not add features to it that the Tauri app lacks unless the
feature is the reason it exists (the unpacker).

## Building it

The shell is a normal CMake target and is on by default:

```powershell
powershell -File tools/build.ps1 -NoFrontend          # builds build\src\app\reverse-slop.exe
```

To build **only** the shell (no engine host, no tests):

```powershell
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release `
      -DSLOP_BUILD_UI=ON -DSLOP_BUILD_ENGINE=OFF -DSLOP_BUILD_TESTS=OFF
cmake --build build --target reverse-slop
```

`SLOP_BUILD_UI=ON` is the default; `-DSLOP_BUILD_UI=OFF` drops `src/ui` and `src/app` from
the build entirely (CI builds the engine and the Tauri app, so the shell only has to keep
compiling).

Output: `build\src\app\reverse-slop.exe`.

## Views

Registered in `src/ui/panels.cpp` (`RegisterBuiltins`), with these shortcuts:

| View | Shortcut | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Targets | `Ctrl+1` | process list, attach, PS4 connect |
| Inspector | `Ctrl+2` | placeholder in this shell (the Tauri app has the real one) |
| Disassembly | `Ctrl+3` | function list + instruction view |
| Pseudocode | `Ctrl+0` | decompiler output with jump-back navigation |
| Memory | `Ctrl+4` | regions + hex editor |
| Output | `Ctrl+5` | engine log |
| Scanner | `Ctrl+6` | value scanner |
| Strings | `Ctrl+7` | string index |
| Image Browser | `Ctrl+8` | sections/imports/exports |
| Debugger | `Ctrl+9` | PS4 breakpoints, watchpoints, registers, events, remote calls |
| Unpacker | — | Magicmida job UI (hidden by default) |
| Frame Metrics | `F12` | ImGui draw stats (debug) |

Plus a command palette (`src/ui/command_palette.cpp`), docking and three themes
(Obsidian, Nord-slop, Blood-orange).

## Feature parity

Derived from `src/ui/panels.cpp` + `src/ui/view_*.cpp` versus
`app/src/components/**` (ActivityRail, WorkspacePanel tabs, panels/). "MCP" means the
feature is reachable from the Tauri app through an agent or `/api`, not through its own
widget.

| Feature | ImGui shell | Tauri app | Gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Targets / attach | yes | yes | — |
| PS4 connect + payload card | connect popup only | full card (send/save/check/download) | ImGui has no payload card |
| Modules list | yes (table inside Targets, with dump + analyze) | **Modules** panel | — |
| Inspector | placeholder text | full inspector | ImGui inspector is a stub |
| Scanner | yes | yes | — |
| Watchlist + freeze | yes | yes | — |
| Memory / hex editor | yes | yes | — |
| Disassembly | yes | yes | — |
| Strings | yes | yes | — |
| Image Browser (PE) | yes | yes | — |
| Decompiler (pseudocode) | **yes** (Pseudocode view) | no widget (MCP `decomp.function` / Lua) | Tauri has no pseudocode pane |
| Debugger (PS4) | yes | yes | — |
| Local debugger composites | no widget | no widget | both are MCP-only |
| Xray / patch / devirt / emulate | no widget | no widget | MCP-only on both |
| Magicmida unpacker | **yes** (Unpacker view) | no widget (MCP `devirt.themida_*`) | Tauri has no unpacker UI |
| Lua scripts | no | **yes** (Scripts panel) | ImGui has no script surface |
| Command palette | yes | yes (`Ctrl+K`) | — |
| Output panel | yes | yes | — |
| Settings UI | no (edit `settings.json`) | **yes** (Settings modal) | ImGui has no settings UI |
| MCP token rotation | no | yes | ImGui has no settings UI |
| Auto-update | no | **yes** (Tauri updater) | ImGui has no updater |
| MCP client onboarding | no | yes (engine-side, shared) | the engine does it for both |
| Themes | 3 | 5 (+Daylight, High contrast) | ImGui has no light theme |
| Frame metrics | yes (`F12`) | no | debug-only |
| E2E / screenshots | no | yes (`app/e2e`) | screenshots come from the Tauri UI |

The two "Tauri lacks it" rows are the honest ones: the pseudocode pane and the unpacker UI
exist only in the ImGui shell. Both are reachable in the Tauri app through MCP, so no
capability is lost — only a widget.

# SlopStation

**PS4 reverse-engineering workbench** — live memory, scanning and debugging over
ps4debug-NG · static analysis of dumped modules · a decompiler and x86-64 emulator ·
Lua scripting · a built-in MCP server for AI agents.

![SlopStation workspace: host process list, value scanner and watchlist, disassembly of a loaded PE, inspector](screenshots/workspace.png)

SlopStation is a Windows workbench for PS4 reverse engineering and game research. It
speaks the [ps4debug-NG](https://github.com/Pharaoh2k/ps4debug-NG) wire protocol directly,
runs the same analysis stack against local Windows processes, and exposes everything —
live memory, the debugger, the scanner, the decompiler, the emulator, the network tools —
through one UI, one Lua surface and one MCP server.

> **Scope.** Use SlopStation only on consoles, games, and systems you own or are
> authorized to test. Live debugging and memory writes can crash the console or the game.
> Host-side packet capture needs administrator rights on the analysis PC. See
> [Security and qualification](project/security.md).

| build it from source | [Building](project/building.md) |
| load your own code on the console | [Injection recipes](injection/README.md) |

```md
# Loading your own code on a jailbroken PS4 (homebrew recipes)

Condensed from the ps4-injection-lab method table. These are for **your own
homebrew payloads** on hardware you own. The kernel/DMA/controller-spoof
methods (07, 14–19) and the cheat-XML method (10) are intentionally not
covered — they exist for anti-cheat evasion, not development.

| # | Method | Use it when | PS4-side scope | Persistent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `CMD_PROC_ELF` (`ps4_elf_load` in the debugger tool) | run a freestanding ELF in the game process now | freestanding ELF | until crash |
| 02 | `CMD_PROC_ELF_RPC` (`ps4_elf_rpc`) | same, with a deferred entry point | freestanding ELF | until crash |
| 03 | `CMD_PROC_INTALL` + `CMD_PROC_CALL` (`ps4_call`) | call one function with args, get rax | none (host-driven) | no |
| 04 | GoldHEN SPRX plugin | load a proper `.sprx` plugin into the game | SPRX plugin | game session |
| 05 | `sceKernelLoadStartModule` via RPC | load an SPRX from a stub ELF | stub ELF + SPRX | game session |
| 06 | custom BinLoader daemon (port 7777) | repeated loads without re-sending the ELF | custom daemon | until reboot |
| 08 | SELF + GoldHEN patch XML | patch the game's own code/data on disk | none | until game update |
| 09 | elfldr (port 9021) | classic payload loader | freestanding ELF | until crash |
| 11 | fake PKG sidecar | run as a real PS4 application | PS4 application | app launcher |
| 12 | SPRX hotswap | swap a loaded module at runtime | ELF + replacement SPRX | game session |
| 13 | shared-memory sidecar | game↔sidecar IPC channel | ELF + sidecar | game session |

## From the MCP server

```
target.ps4_discover                      # or ps4_connect {host:"auto"}
target.ps4_auto {host}                   # connect + pick game + attach + debug
debugger.ps4_elf_load {path}             # method 01, your own ELF
debugger.ps4_call {addr, args:[...]}     # method 03
host.start {port:9090, bind:"0.0.0.0", token:"..."}   # serve payloads to the console
```

Serve your payload with the `host` tool, then load it on the console with
method 09 (elfldr) or 01 (`ps4_elf_load`). Every load is a mutating action:
with `mcp_require_confirm` on it needs `"confirm": true`, and every call is
in the JSONL audit log.

Full mechanism docs, protocol details and failure modes for each method live
in the ps4-injection-lab repository (`NN-<name>/README.md` per method).

`docs/linux.md`:

```md
# Linux (x86-64) engine

The headless engine (`reverse-slop-engine`) builds and runs on Linux. The
window shell (`reverse-slop.exe`, DX11/ImGui) is Windows-only and is not part
of this build.

## Build

```sh
sudo apt-get install -y cmake ninja-build g++ libssl-dev
cmake -S . -B build-linux -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build-linux --target reverse-slop-engine slop_tests
```

Dependencies (zydis, fmt, spdlog, capstone, zlib, cpp-httplib, Unicorn, SQLite,
Lua, nlohmann/json) are fetched into `_ext/` exactly as on Windows. OpenSSL is
the system package.

## Run

```sh
./build-linux/src/engine/reverse-slop-engine --no-onboard --port 8799
# SLOP_ENGINE_READY 8799 <token>
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8799/health
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}' http://127.0.0.1:8799/mcp
```

State lives under `$XDG_DATA_HOME/reverse-slop` (default
`~/.local/share/reverse-slop`). `--stdio` works the same as on Windows.

## What works

| Area | Notes |
|---|---|
| MCP server (`/health`, `/api/v1`, `/mcp`) | httplib, unchanged |
| `target.*` local processes | `/proc` enumeration, modules from `/proc/pid/maps`, threads from `/proc/pid/task` |
| `memory.*` read/write | `process_vm_readv`/`process_vm_writev`, fallback `/proc/<pid>/mem` |
| `disasm.*`, `analysis.*`, `re.*` | Hyperion + Zydis/capstone, same code as Windows |
| `script.*` (Lua) | Lua 5.4 built as C++ with `LUA_USE_POSIX` |
| `emu.*` | Unicorn builds on Linux |
| `fs.*`, `web.*` | `std::filesystem`; HTTPS through OpenSSL |
| localhost HTTP proxy | plain HTTP + CONNECT; upstream TLS via OpenSSL |
| packet capture | `AF_PACKET` raw sockets; needs `CAP_NET_RAW` (not exercised by the WSL checks) |
| PS4/PS5 backends | the ps4debug/ps5debug wire protocol is platform-neutral; only the socket layer was ported. Exercised by the fake-server tests |

## Gated, and why

| Area | Behaviour on Linux |
|---|---|
| Local debugger (`debugger` local actions) | Win32 debug API only; `attach` reports that. Use a console backend. |
| Thread contexts, handle tables | `ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED`; `/proc` has no equivalent of `GetThreadContext` |
| `protect`/`alloc`/`free` on another process | `ERROR_NOT_SUPPORTED`; `mprotect`/`mmap` only affect this address space, so they work for the engine's own pid |
| MITM TLS interception | needs a local CA in a certificate store (CNG). `mitm.*` reports that; plain HTTP proxying still works |
| Server-side TLS (`tls_stream::accept`) | same reason; the client side is implemented with OpenSSL |
| Process icons | no shell icon extraction; the UI draws its generic glyph |
| Heap enumeration | Toolhelp only; `heap.*` reports that |
| Magicmida unpack | the sidecar is a Windows PE; `analyze.unpack` reports that |
| MCP onboarding | writes XDG config paths (`~/.claude.json`, `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, `~/.config/Code/User/settings.json`, `~/.config/opencode/config.json`) |

## Verified

Built and run inside WSL (Kali, gcc 16, Release): `reverse-slop-engine` links,
prints `SLOP_ENGINE_READY <port> <token>`, and answers

- `GET /health` -> `{"ok":true,"server":"slopstation","version":"0.2.3"}`
- `tools/list` -> the 22 core tools
- `target.list` -> the WSL processes (`/proc`), `target.attach` -> `backend: "posix"`
- `memory.read` on a spawned `python3` -> the ELF header bytes at `0x400000`
- `disasm.load /bin/ls` -> `format: "elf"`, `functions: 22`, then `disasm.functions`
- `script.run` -> `return: 42`

`slop_tests` (portable subset) passes 97 of 98 cases. The one failure,
`ps4_debug_port_in_use_names_owner`, needs `/proc/net/tcp`, which this WSL
kernel reports empty; it passes on a normal Linux host.

## Privileges

- Cross-process memory access needs `CAP_SYS_PTRACE` (or a parent/child
  relationship; `kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=1` otherwise denies it).
- Packet capture needs `CAP_NET_RAW`; `network.capture_start` reports the
  missing capability instead of failing silently.

## Tests

`slop_tests` on Linux builds a portable subset: `ipa`, `emu`, `ps4`,
`ps4_chaos`, `ps4_debug`, `ps5`, `disasm_accuracy`. The other areas need
`SlopTarget.exe` or Win32 APIs and stay Windows-only.
