`docs/project/architecture.md`:

```md
# Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph PC["Analysis PC (Windows)"]
    UI["Tauri v2 + React<br/>app/"] -- "/api, /events (HTTP + SSE)" --> ENG
    AG["AI agent / MCP client"] -- "/mcp (JSON-RPC)" --> ENG
    IMGUI["ImGui / DX11 shell<br/>src/app + src/ui"] -- in-process --> CORE
    subgraph ENG["reverse-slop-engine.exe (src/engine)"]
      CORE["slop_core (src/core)<br/>process · memory · disasm · analysis<br/>emu · network · script · mcp"]
      HYPE["Hyperion<br/>src/hyperion"]
      CORE --- HYPE
    end
  end
  CORE -- "TCP 744 commands" --> PS4["PS4 running ps4debug-NG"]
  PS4 -- "TCP 755 debug events" --> CORE
```

- The Tauri supervisor (`app/src-tauri`) starts the engine as a sidecar, waits for the
  `SLOP_ENGINE_READY <port> <token>` handshake (up to 180 s, covering the UAC prompt),
  holds it in a kill-on-close job object and lets it shut down cleanly. Keeping the engine
  out of the Rust process avoids CRT mixing and isolates crashes.
- Both hosts share the lifecycle in `src/core/infra/lifecycle.cpp`: paths and worker
  queues → process/target services → settings and persistence → MCP/API server and
  onboarding → periodic target/watch/event servicing → orderly shutdown.
- Without a console, the active backend is the Win32 user-mode backend (`OpenProcess` /
  `ReadProcessMemory`) — the same one the test fixture drives.

## Layout

```text
src/
├── app/       Win32 entry + DX11 loop (legacy shell)
├── engine/    headless host and parent-process contract
├── ui/        ImGui chrome, docking, theme, views
├── hyperion/  vendored analysis/decompiler engine (hype namespace)
├── core/
│   ├── infra/     lifecycle, jobs, settings, paths, events, onboarding
│   ├── runtime/   ps4debug-NG backend + Win32 user-mode backend
│   ├── process/   targets, processes, modules, threads, dumps
│   ├── memory/    scanner, AOB, pointer scan, snapshots, watch service
│   ├── debugger/  call-stack unwinding, local Win32 debugger, composite flows
│   ├── disasm/    image loading, Zydis/Capstone indexes, Hyperion bridge
│   ├── analysis/  packer, signatures, xray, patches, devirt, Magicmida
│   ├── emu/       Unicorn execution and taint
│   ├── network/   raw capture, traffic store, proxy, WinHTTP
│   ├── script/    Lua engine
│   ├── mcp/       JSON-RPC/SSE server and the action-based tool surface
│   ├── persist/   SQLite snapshots and key/value storage
│   └── util/      filesystem, zip, PE helpers
├── target/    SlopTarget fixture (test process)
└── tests/     CTest areas and the fake ps4debug-NG server
```

## One session, three surfaces

The engine owns a single active session (target, image, debugger, watchlist). The UI talks
to it over `/api` and `/events`, agents over `/mcp`, scripts through the Lua engine. That is
why a rename made in the Disassembly tab shows up in `disasm.symbols` from an agent, and why
two clients cannot disagree about which process is attached.

## Threading

- One tool mutex serializes tool calls that touch shared state; long-running work
  (emulation, scanning, Hyperion analysis) runs outside it so the UI keeps answering.
- The watch service samples at about 10 Hz on its own tick; the UI never polls.
- The ps4debug debug-event listener drains each TCP 755 connection on its own thread.

```

`docs/project/building.md`:

```md
# Building

`tools/build.ps1` finds Visual Studio with `vswhere`, uses its bundled CMake and Ninja,
configures the `ninja-msvc-release` preset into `build/`, then builds the Tauri app.
First configure downloads pinned dependencies into `_ext/` (ImGui, FreeType, Zydis,
Capstone, Unicorn, nlohmann/json, cpp-httplib, SQLite, Lua, fmt, spdlog, zlib).

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/NetVar1337/SlopStation.git
cd SlopStation
powershell -File tools/build.ps1          # engine + Tauri app (portable + installer)
powershell -File tools/build.ps1 -NoFrontend   # C++ only, fastest loop
```

| Switch | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| _(none)_ | C++ engine + Tauri app: single-file portable (`dist\SlopStation\`) + per-user NSIS installer |
| `-NoFrontend` | C++ targets only |
| `-FullClean` | Delete `build/` before configuring |
| `-PlanOnly` | Configure without compiling |
| `-Preset <name>` | `ninja-msvc-debug`, `ninja-msvc-asan`, `ninja-msvc-analyze` |
| `-Test` | Build and run the CTest areas (`-TestLabel`, `-TestExclude`, `-TestJobs`) |
| `-Full` | Self-contained installer: embeds WebView2 and Magicmida |
| `-FrontendOnly` / `-BundleOnly` / `-FastBundle` | frontend binary, then bundling only |
| `-OnlineWebview` | use the online WebView2 bootstrapper |
| `-CmakeExtra`, `-Targets`, `-VsRoot` | extra CMake args, target subset, explicit VS root |

`SLOP_BUILD_DIR` moves the binary directory (useful off a virtual or overlay drive).

## CMake options

First-party targets compile with `/W4 /WX`.

| CMake option | Default | Builds |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `SLOP_BUILD_ENGINE` | `ON` | headless engine |
| `SLOP_BUILD_UI` | `ON` | legacy ImGui shell |
| `SLOP_BUILD_TEST_TARGET` | `ON` | `SlopTarget.exe` fixture |
| `SLOP_BUILD_TESTS` | `ON` | `slop_tests.exe` |

`SLOP_ANALYZE=ON` runs MSVC `/analyze`; `SLOP_SANITIZE=address` builds with ASan.

## Payload

The bundled payload is fetched from the latest ps4debug-NG release before packaging:

```powershell
powershell -File tools/fetch_ps4debug.ps1          # latest release -> build/ps4debug-ng
powershell -File tools/fetch_ps4debug.ps1 -Force   # re-download
```

## Outputs

```text
build\src\engine\reverse-slop-engine.exe                     headless engine
build\src\app\reverse-slop.exe                               legacy ImGui shell
dist\SlopStation\SlopStation.exe                            portable single file (engine embedded by CI)
app\src-tauri\target\release\bundle\nsis\...-setup.exe       per-user installer
app\src-tauri\target\release\bundle\nsis\...-setup.exe.sig   updater signature (when the signing key is set)
```

## Versioning

`VERSION` is the single product version; `tools/sync_version.ps1` copies it into the
frontend/Tauri manifests and the README badge, and CI verifies the tag matches
(`tools/sync_version.ps1 -Check -Tag <tag>`).

## CI

- **PRs** run only the lanes their paths touch: C++ build/tests for `src/**`, frontend
  build/tests for `app/**`, and the docs build for `docs/**`.
- **main** runs the build + test + frontend gate. ASan, `/analyze` and clang-tidy run
  nightly (and on manual dispatch), off the push critical path.
- **Tags** use a separate release workflow: it downloads the successful main build's engine
  and frontend artifacts for the same commit, then packages, signs and publishes the
  installer, the single-file portable zip, `SHA256SUMS` and `latest.json` — no rebuild on
  the release path.

## Docs site

The site is mdBook over `docs/`:

```powershell
cargo install mdbook --locked
mdbook serve --open      # http://localhost:3000
mdbook build             # -> docs/book/
```

`.github/workflows/docs.yml` builds it on every PR that touches `docs/**` and deploys to
GitHub Pages from `main`.

`docs/project/security.md`:

```md
# Security and qualification

- The engine binds `127.0.0.1` only and requires a bearer token on `/mcp` and `/api`.
  Mutating tools can require confirmation (`mcp_require_confirm`), and every call is
  written to a JSONL audit log with secrets redacted.
- Live writes and `script.run` are code execution against the target; a bad write can
  crash the console or the game. Read
  [`SECURITY.md`](https://github.com/NetVar1337/SlopStation/blob/main/SECURITY.md) and the
  [audit](../AUDIT.md) before running untrusted payloads or scripts.
- Host packet capture needs administrator rights; TLS interception is opt-in and
  reversible.
- The app's auto-updater verifies the installer against the embedded Tauri public key; the
  private key is a CI secret and never ships.
- Outbound `web` calls do not inherit browser cookies, and private/loopback targets are
  denied unless explicitly allowed.
- `fs` refuses the engine's own data directory, so a script cannot rewrite the session
  database or the token store.

## Qualification

Use SlopStation only on consoles, games, and systems you own or are authorized to test.
The repository's scope rule is the same one the [merge plan](../MERGE.md) states: homebrew
payloads, your own debug builds, your own dumps. Anything whose purpose is cheating in live
online games, evading bans, or circumventing licensing is out of scope.

## Reporting

Security issues go through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting on the repository, not
a public issue — see `SECURITY.md` for the current contact and the supported versions.

```

# Tests

.\build\tests\slop_tests.exe                       # full suite
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure         # registered CTest subsets
$env:SLOP_TEST_FILTER = 'ps4'; .\build\tests\slop_tests.exe; Remove-Item Env:SLOP_TEST_FILTER

Areas are `src/tests/test_<area>.cpp` against the harness in `harness.hpp`; one executable,
`slop_tests.exe`. `SLOP_TEST_AREA` selects one area, `SLOP_TEST_FILTER` filters by name.

The PS4 tests run the backend and the `ps4_*` MCP flows against a fake ps4debug-NG server
on loopback, including chaos modes (fragmented replies, mid-transfer disconnects) and the
reconnect/slot-restore flows.

Other suites cover infrastructure, memory, disassembly, MCP wire/schemas, analysis,
emulation, the capture store, persistence, RTTI/types, Lua, module dumping,
Hyperion/decompilation, Mach-O/`.ipa`, Xray/patching and Magicmida supervision.

## The fixture

`SlopTarget.exe` (`src/target`) is a real process with known values, a pointer chain, an
AOB fixture set, a region zoo and a mutator, so tests (and the screenshots) can attach to
something deterministic. Its console commands (`tick`, `auto <hz>`, `set <name> <val>`,
`mutate`, `report`, …) let a human drive it by hand.

## End-to-end

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `node app/e2e/run.mjs smoke` | API battery: health, attach, read, watchlist, script, detach |
| `node app/e2e/run.mjs screenshots` | regenerates `docs/screenshots/*.png` from the real UI |
| `python tools/mcp_stdio_test.py` | stdio JSON-RPC session against the engine |
| `python tools/mcp_live_test.py` | HTTP battery against a running engine |

CI runs `smoke` in the nightly `tests` lane; screenshots mode is manual (image-compare
flakiness).

[Benchmarks](../benchmarks/README.md).

`docs/ps5.md`:

```md
# PS5 console backend (ps5debug-NG)

SlopStation can drive a jailbroken PS5 running the **ps5debug-NG** payload the
same way it drives a local process: process list, attach, memory read/write,
VM maps, module list, live debugging (breakpoints, watchpoints, registers,
continue/step) and console notifications.

## Protocol source

Implemented against **ps5debug-NG v1.3.2**:

- repository: <https://github.com/Pharaoh2k/ps5debug-NG>
- commit: `a1a6cb2dae7544f892454f62046b7f70500ffa8e` (2026-10-22)
- references: `common/include/protocol.h` and `PROTOCOL.md`

ps5debug-NG descends from golden's ps4debug, so the framing is identical to
ps4debug-NG's: a 12-byte `{magic, cmd, datalen}` header (`magic =
0xFFAABBCC`) followed by `datalen` raw body bytes, every field little-endian
and every struct packed. The vm_map entry (58 bytes) and the port-755 stop
packet (0x4A0 bytes) are byte-identical to ps4debug's, which is why the
backend reuses the PS4 segment/module grouping and stop-event decoder.

Differences from the PS4 backend that matter:

| Topic | ps5debug-NG |
|-------|-------------|
| Status words | bit-swapped on the wire; the client compares `CMD_SUCCESS = 0x80000000`, `CMD_ERROR = 0xF0000001`, `CMD_DATA_NULL = 0xF0000003`, `CMD_ALREADY_DEBUG = 0xF0000004`, `CMD_INVALID_INDEX = 0xF0000005` |
| Read/write streaming | 64 KiB chunks (`NET_MAX_LENGTH` is 8192 payload-side) |
| `CMD_DEBUG_ATTACH` body | 4 bytes (`pid` only; the payload takes the client IP from the connection slot) |
| Module list | none server-side: modules are grouped from `CMD_PROC_MAPS` by backing file |
| Unknown opcode | `CMD_ERROR` **and the payload closes the client**, so the backend never probes for commands it does not need |
| Auth | `CMD_PROC_AUTH` only gates the on-console scan trio; this backend does not use those commands (the generic scanner reads memory instead), so no auth handshake is performed |
| Watchpoint length | the payload wants the DR7 length field (0=1, 1=2, 2=8, 3=4 bytes), not a byte count; the backend converts |

## Ports

| Port | Proto | Direction | Purpose |
|------|-------|-----------|---------|
| 744 | TCP | PC → console | command server (`target.ps5_connect`) |
| 755 | TCP | console → PC | stop events; the backend listens and pins the peer to the console it attached to |
| 1010 | UDP | broadcast | discovery (`host: "auto"`), magic `0xFFFFAAAA` |

## Commands used

| Command | ID | Backend use |
|---------|----|-------------|
| `CMD_VERSION` | `0xBD000001` | handshake: protocol version string |
| `CMD_FW_VERSION` | `0xBD000500` | handshake: firmware as `major*100+minor` (900 = 9.00) |
| `CMD_BRANDING` | `0xBD000501` | handshake: brand + `NUL` + capability level |
| `CMD_PLATFORM_ID` | `0xBD000502` | handshake: must answer 5 (PS5), else the connect is refused |
| `CMD_PROC_NOP` | `0xBDAACC06` | `ping()` and the handshake liveness probe |
| `CMD_PROC_LIST` | `0xBDAA0001` | `target.list` |
| `CMD_PROC_INFO` | `0xBDAA000A` | attach validation, name/path |
| `CMD_PROC_READ` / `CMD_PROC_WRITE` | `0xBDAA0002/3` | `memory.read`/`memory.write` and the generic scanner |
| `CMD_PROC_MAPS` | `0xBDAA0004` | `target.regions`, `target.modules`, read-coverage checks |
| `CMD_PROC_PROTECT` | `0xBDAA0008` | `memory.protect` |
| `CMD_PROC_ALLOC` / `CMD_PROC_ALLOC_HINTED` / `CMD_PROC_FREE` | `0xBDAA000B/0E/0C` | `memory.alloc`/`memory.free` |
| `CMD_DEBUG_ATTACH` / `CMD_DEBUG_DETACH` | `0xBDBB0001/2` | `debugger.ps5_attach`/`ps5_detach` |
| `CMD_DEBUG_SET_BREAKPOINT` / `CMD_DEBUG_SET_WATCHPOINT` | `0xBDBB0003/4` | `ps5_bp_set`/`ps5_watch_set` (30 software / 4 hardware slots) |
| `CMD_DEBUG_GET_THREAD_LIST` / `CMD_DEBUG_THREAD_INFO` | `0xBDBB0005/11` | `target.threads`, `debugger.ps5_threads` |
| `CMD_DEBUG_GETREGS` / `CMD_DEBUG_SETREGS` | `0xBDBB0008/9` | `ps5_regs`, `ps5_set_reg` |
| `CMD_DEBUG_CONTINUE` / `CMD_DEBUG_STEP` / `CMD_DEBUG_STEP_THREAD` | `0xBDBB0010/12/13` | `ps5_continue`, `ps5_step` |
| `CMD_DEBUG_SUSPEND` / `CMD_DEBUG_RESUME` | `0xBDBB0006/7` | `ps5_suspend`/`ps5_resume` |
| `CMD_CONSOLE_NOTIFY` / `CMD_CONSOLE_PRINT` | `0xBDDD0004/3` | `target.ps5_notify`, `debugger.ps5_print` |
| `CMD_CONSOLE_INFO` / `CMD_CONSOLE_FOREGROUND_APP` | `0xBDDD0005/6` | `ps5_console_info`, `ps5_app` |

## MCP surface

`target`:

- `ps5_connect {host, port=744, pid?}` — handshake + optional attach; `host:
  "auto"` uses the UDP discovery probe.
- `ps5_disconnect`, `ps5_reconnect` (re-handshake, re-attach the debuggee,
  re-arm every breakpoint/watchpoint), `ps5_auto {host}` (connect, pick the
  process whose maps live under `/app0/`, attach, debug-attach),
  `ps5_notify {msg}`.
- `status` adds a `ps5` block (endpoint, branding, server version, caps, fw,
  platform, connected/lost, drops, debug state).
- `list`, `attach`, `modules`, `regions`, `threads`, `memory.*`, `disasm.*`,
  `memory.scan`/`aob` work through the backend abstraction unchanged once a
  PS5 is the active backend.

`debugger`:

- `ps5_status`, `ps5_attach`, `ps5_detach`, `ps5_console_info`,
  `ps5_bp_set`/`ps5_bp_clear`/`ps5_bp_list`,
  `ps5_watch_set`/`ps5_watch_clear`/`ps5_watch_list`,
  `ps5_continue`, `ps5_step`, `ps5_suspend`, `ps5_resume`, `ps5_regs`,
  `ps5_set_reg`, `ps5_threads`, `ps5_wait`, `ps5_events`, `ps5_notify`,
  `ps5_print`, `ps5_app`.

## Limits

- **No on-console scan engine.** ps5debug-NG's `CMD_PROC_SCAN*` family needs
  the `CMD_PROC_AUTH` challenge-response and only accepts four-byte-relative
  result offsets; this backend does not implement it. `memory.scan`, `aob`
  and pointer scans stream memory over the wire instead (correct, slower).
  `engine=console` is therefore rejected for PS5.
- **No remote function call / ELF upload / on-device disasm / snapshot.**
  Those ps4debug-NG commands are not part of the ps5debug-NG v1.3.2 surface
  this backend targets (it deliberately does not probe unknown opcodes, since
  the payload closes the client on one).
- **No `target.ps5_dump_module`.** `target.dump_module` is PE-only; dump PS5
  modules with `memory.read` over the `target.modules` ranges (or wait for a
  follow-up slice).
- **Threads need a debug session.** The payload only lists lwpids while
  attached, so `target.threads` on a PS5 fails with "no ps5 debug session"
  until `debugger.ps5_attach`.
- **One console at a time.** Connecting a PS5 drops a selected PS4 and vice
  versa; the registry swaps the active backend and detaches the session first.
- **A failed command usually drops the connection** (the payload closes the
  client on handler failure). The backend then reports `connected=false`,
  `lost=true` and a reason; `target.ps5_reconnect` re-runs the handshake,
  re-attaches the debuggee and re-arms the slots. There is no transparent
  reconnect: unlike the PS4 backend, the next call fails fast instead of
  re-opening behind the caller's back.
- Firmware coverage is whatever ps5debug-NG v1.3.2 supports (the payload does
  its own firmware-specific kernel work); the backend only reports the
  firmware number it announces.

## Tests

`src/tests/test_ps5.cpp` runs against `src/tests/ps5_fixture.hpp`, a fake
ps5debug-NG payload on loopback TCP that implements the command subset above,
the port-755 connect-back and fault injection (fragmented replies, a byte
budget that cuts the connection mid-reply, a silent command, a non-status
word). Areas: `SLOP_TEST_AREA=ps5`.

```

`docs/tutorials/dump-rename-decompile.md`:

```md
# Tutorial: dump a module, rename it, decompile it

Goal: take a game module off a live console, turn it into a loadable ELF, and work on it
with the static tools — function index, xrefs, strings, renames, comments, the decompiler,
Xray passes and patching with a journal.

Prerequisite: a connected console with an attached process
([First console connect](first-console-connect.md)).

## 1. Dump the module

From the UI: **Debugger** → the dump row at the bottom. Type the module name in
**Module to dump** (`eboot.bin` by default), pick an output path with the folder button
(**Dump output path**), then press **dump+load**.

From an agent, the same thing in one call:

```json
{ "tool": "target", "action": "ps4_dump_module",
  "params": { "name": "eboot.bin", "path": "C:/dumps/eboot.bin.elf", "load": true } }
```

What the parameters mean:

| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` or `base` | — | module to dump, by exact name or by runtime base (one is required) |
| `path` | — | output file (required) |
| `format` | `elf` when `load` is true, else `raw` | `raw` is the mapped span with gaps zero-filled; `elf` rebuilds an ELF64 with one `PT_LOAD` per console segment at its runtime VA |
| `load` | `false` | load the result into the shared image session as soon as it is written |
| `strict` | `false` | fail on unreadable pages instead of zero-filling them |

`load: true` requires `format: "elf"` — a raw span has no ELF headers to load. The engine
loads the dump at the module's runtime base and **does not** apply relocations, because the
bytes were already relocated in memory.

The reply tells you what happened:

```json
{ "dumped": true, "complete": true, "format": "elf", "path": "C:/dumps/eboot.bin.elf",
  "bytes_written": 41943040, "segment_count": 3, "loaded": true,
  "module": { "base": "0x200000000", "name": "eboot.bin", "path": "/app0/eboot.bin" },
  "warnings": [] }
```

`complete: false` means some pages could not be read and were zero-filled — the analysis is
still usable, but code in those pages is missing. `loaded: false` comes with a `load_note`
explaining why.

## 2. Wait for analysis, then look at functions

```json
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "loaded", "params": {} }
```

Poll until `image.ready` and `image.hype.ready` are true; the decompiler and the analyzer
database need the background Hyperion pass. `image.format` is `elf` for a dump.

```json
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "functions", "params": { "limit": 50, "filter": "player" } }
```

`functions` returns `va`, `name`, `size`, plus Hyperion's CFG stats once analysis is done.
`filter` matches names and addresses (`0x4DDA48` and `4dda48` both work), `limit` is capped
at 10000.

In the UI the same list is the **Disassembly** tab: virtualized, flow-coloured, click a
row to follow jumps.

![Disassembly of a loaded image](../screenshots/disassembly.png)

## 3. Strings and xrefs

```json
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "strings", "params": { "min": 6, "limit": 200 } }
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "xrefs", "params": { "addr": "0x2004DDA48", "limit": 100 } }
```

`strings` takes a minimum length and an exec-section filter; `xrefs` answers "who
references this address" from the Hyperion database, augmented on x86/x64 with the legacy
index and a RIP-relative `LEA` sweep, and reports which engines contributed.

The **Strings** tab is the same index with min-length and exec-section filters; click a
string to follow its xrefs.

![String index with filters](../screenshots/strings.png)

## 4. Rename and comment

Rename a function in the UI: double-click its name in the Disassembly list (or select it
and press `F2`), type, `Enter`. The rename is saved and every surface sees it.

From an agent:

```json
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "symbol_set",
  "params": { "addr": "0x2004DDA48", "name": "Player::apply_damage" } }
```

`symbol_set` writes a **user** symbol; an empty `name` clears it. `disasm.symbols` lists
user renames next to analyzer names with `source: "user" | "hyperion"`, and user names win.
Renames persist per file hash, so they survive a reload and remap across bases.

Comments are an API/Lua surface (neither desktop shell renders them yet):

```json
{ "tool": "notes", "action": "set_comment",
  "params": { "addr": "0x2004DDA48", "text": "called from the damage path" } }
{ "tool": "notes", "action": "comments", "params": {} }
```

`notes.bookmark_toggle` / `notes.bookmarks` do the same for bookmarks. Both persist per
file hash like renames.

## 5. Decompile

```json
{ "tool": "decomp", "action": "function", "params": { "addr": "0x2004DDA48" } }
```

`decomp.function` waits up to 10 s for the Hyperion analysis, then returns C-like output
lifted through p-code, SSA, DCE, type inference and structuring. It fails clearly when the
image has no Hyperion engine (unsupported format) or the analysis errored — re-run
`disasm.load` to restart it.

Related calls on the same database:

```json
{ "tool": "decomp", "action": "function", "params": { "addr": "0x2004DDA48" } }
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "blocks", "params": { "addr": "0x2004DDA48" } }
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "globals", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "disasm", "action": "vtables", "params": {} }
```

## 6. Xray passes

Xray is read-only and works on the loaded image. The useful ones on a fresh dump:

```json
{ "tool": "xray", "action": "obfuscation", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "xray", "action": "cff", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "xray", "action": "strings_recon", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "xray", "action": "indirect_calls", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "xray", "action": "gadgets", "params": {} }
```

| Action | Answers |
| --- | --- |
| `cfg`, `complexity` | control-flow graph and cyclomatic complexity |
| `cff` | control-flow flattening detection |
| `obfuscation` | aggregate obfuscation score |
| `strings_recon` | reconstructed stack/immediate strings |
| `indirect_calls` | recovered indirect-call targets |
| `anti_analysis` | anti-debug/anti-VM patterns (PE only) |
| `hooks`, `syscalls` | inline hooks and direct syscalls |
| `apihash` | API-hash resolution |
| `entropy`, `pages`, `crypto_range` | entropy windows, page classification, crypto constants |
| `gadgets` | ROP gadgets |

## 7. Patch, and keep the journal

Patching works on the loaded image only, and every byte change is journaled so it can be
reverted.

```json
{ "tool": "patch", "action": "nop_junk", "params": { "addr": "0x2004DDA48" } }
{ "tool": "patch", "action": "journal", "params": { "limit": 100 } }
{ "tool": "patch", "action": "revert_all", "params": {} }
```

`journal` returns `patches[]` (`va`, `before`, `after`), `total` and `indexes_dirty`.
`revert_all` restores every recorded byte. The indexes rebuild lazily after a patch, so
`disasm.functions`/`xrefs`/`strings` stay correct.

Other passes: `resolve_opaque`, `patch_antidebug` (PE), `unpack_xor`, `decode_strings`,
`write_bytes {addr, hex}`, `full_pass` (combined, reports the obfuscation-score reduction),
`rebuild` (re-disassemble after edits).

## 8. Keep going

- [Static analysis](../features/static-analysis.md) — the full picture of what the image
  session holds.
- [Decompiler](../features/decompiler.md) — what the output means.
- [Live memory](../features/live-memory.md) — take an address from the dump back to the
  running game.

```

`docs/tutorials/first-console-connect.md`:

```md
# Tutorial: first console connect

Goal: from a cold start to a live, debuggable game process on a PS4 you own, and know what
each failure looks like.

What you need:

- A PS4 on the same LAN, jailbroken, with GoldHEN (or any loader) available.
- SlopStation installed or built (see [Install](../getting-started/install.md)).
- The console IP. If you do not know it, **Discover** will find it.

## 1. Open Targets

Launch the app. With no console connected the Targets panel shows the empty state
**Connect a console** with the connect form and the *ps4debug-NG payload* card below it.

![Targets panel with the connect form and the payload card](../screenshots/workspace.png)

## 2. Get the payload onto the console

The payload is ps4debug-NG, the program the engine talks to over TCP 744. The app ships a
copy; the card shows its tag (`v<tag>`) and where it came from.

Two ways to get it running:

**Send it over BinLoader.** GoldHEN listens for a payload on TCP 9090. The card's port
field defaults to `9090`; press **Send to console**. The engine opens one fresh TCP
connection, streams the raw `.bin` and closes it. The card reports
`Sent <bytes> bytes to <host>:<port>.` The loader then executes the payload, which starts
listening on 744.

**Save it and load it yourself.** **Save payload…** writes the `.bin` wherever you want —
FTP it to `/data/` and load it with a payload manager, or use a GoldHEN `/data/payload.bin`
autoload. The same bytes work either way.

If the bundled build is older than the newest GitHub release, **Check latest** compares
them and shows **Download v\<tag\>**; downloading stores it under
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\dev.slopstation.ui\payloads\ps4debug-ng\`.

The same steps from an agent:

```json
{ "tool": "target", "action": "ps4_send_payload",
  "params": { "host": "192.168.1.50", "port": 9090 } }
```

`path` is optional — without it the engine uses the bundled payload next to the executable
or in the app data directory. The payload must be ≤ 64 MiB (it is ~1 MiB).

## 3. Discover the console

Press **Discover** in the connect form. The engine broadcasts the 4-byte magic
`0xFFFFAAAA` to `255.255.255.255:1010` and collects every payload that answers with the
same magic (the ps4debug-mcp discovery convention). Answers fill the IP field; when more
than one console answers, each is offered as a link button.

```json
{ "tool": "target", "action": "ps4_discover", "params": { "timeout_ms": 2000 } }
```

returns `found`, `consoles[]` and the probe it used. `timeout_ms` defaults to 2000 and is
capped at 60000.

Discovery is a convenience, not a requirement: type the IP and skip it.

## 4. Connect

Enter the IP (the field is labelled **PS4 IP address**, default port `744`) and press
**Connect**. The engine opens the command connection, reads the payload version and
branding, and starts the debug-event listener on 755.

When it works the panel switches to **PS4 processes** with a banner showing the endpoint
and the payload branding, plus a **Disconnect** button. The list is the console's process
table: PID, name, arch, and an attach action per row.

One call does connect + process pick + attach + debug attach:

```json
{ "tool": "target", "action": "ps4_auto", "params": { "host": "192.168.1.50" } }
```

`ps4_auto` enumerates processes, marks each one that has a module under `/app0/` as a game,
prefers the one whose name contains `eboot`, attaches a session and the ps4debug debugger,
and returns `pid`, `name`, `debug_attached`, `candidates[]`, `modules[]`, `threads[]` and
`region_count`. If nothing has `/app0/` modules it falls back to the process with the
largest total module size and sets `heuristic_pick: true` — check `candidates` before
trusting it.

![Debugger view once a console is attached](../screenshots/debugger.png)

## 5. Confirm you are live

```json
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_status", "params": {} }
```

`debug_attached: true` and a `debug_pid` mean breakpoints, watchpoints and steps work.
Then:

```json
{ "tool": "target", "action": "modules", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "read", "params": { "addr": "0x200001000", "len": 64 } }
```

Reads are validated against the console's VM map, so an unmapped address fails instead of
returning zeros. Everything else — scanning, the decompiler on live addresses, the
debugger — follows from here: see [Live memory](../features/live-memory.md),
[Live debugging](../features/live-debugging.md) and
[On-console tooling](../features/on-console-tooling.md).

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Discover** says *No console answered the discovery probe.* | The payload is not running, has no discovery listener, or the PC is on another subnet/VLAN | Load ps4debug-NG first; type the IP manually if discovery is blocked |
| `connect to <ip>:744 timed out` | Nothing is listening on 744 — payload not loaded, or it crashed | Re-send the payload; check the console's loader log |
| `connect to <ip>:744 failed (WSA …)` | Refused or unreachable | Wrong IP, console asleep, or a firewall between the hosts |
| **Send to console** fails with `connect … :9090` | BinLoader is not listening (GoldHEN not running, or a different loader port) | Start GoldHEN, or change the port field to your loader's port |
| **Send to console** fails with `no payload found` | No bundled payload next to the engine and none downloaded | **Check latest → Download v\<tag\>**, or pass an explicit `path` |
| Connected, but the process list is empty | The payload answered the handshake but the process command failed | Check `debugger.ps4_status` for `fw`; a mismatched payload build can reject commands |
| `ps4_dump_module requires a connected console with an attached process` | The console is connected but no process is attached | Attach a row in Targets, or `target.ps4_connect {host, pid}` |
| Debug attach fails (`debug_attached: false`, `debug_error` set) | The payload refused `CMD_DEBUG_ATTACH`, often because another debugger holds the process | Detach the other debugger (or restart the game), then `ps4_reconnect` |
| Connection drops mid-session | Payload restart, console sleep, or Wi-Fi | `target.ps4_reconnect` — the engine resets debug and turbo-scan sessions and says so in the error text |
| Windows Firewall prompt on first run | The engine listens on 127.0.0.1 and opens outbound sockets | Allow it on private networks; inbound access is not needed for console work |

The debug-event listener on 755 accepts only the console you attached, and each connection
is drained on its own thread, so a stale connection from a previous session cannot inject
events.

```

`docs/tutorials/local-process.md`:

```md
# Tutorial: a local process, no console

Everything in SlopStation except the `ps4_*` actions works against a **local Windows
process** through the user-mode backend (`OpenProcess` / `ReadProcessMemory` /
`WriteProcessMemory`). That is how the test fixture and the screenshots are driven, and it
is the fastest way to learn the scanner and the debugger without a console on the desk.

The bundled fixture is `SlopTarget.exe` (`src/target`), built by
`powershell -File tools/build.ps1 -NoFrontend` into `build/src/app/SlopTarget.exe`.

## 1. Start a target

```powershell
.\build\src\app\SlopTarget.exe
```

It prints its PID and the addresses of its known values (`values.health`, `values.score`,
`values.speed`, `values.gold`, …) and then waits on stdin:

```
commands: tick, auto <hz>, stop, set <name> <val>, inc <name>, dec <name>,
          mutate, realloc, report, regions, quit
>
```

`auto 2` makes it tick twice a second: health decreases, score increases by 10, speed
drifts by 0.01. That gives the scanner something to narrow against.

Any other process works too — a game, a debug build of your own code. The backend needs
`PROCESS_VM_READ | PROCESS_VM_WRITE | PROCESS_VM_OPERATION | PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION`
on it, so same-user processes are fine and protected/elevated ones need an elevated
SlopStation.

## 2. Attach

In **Targets**, click **“List this PC's processes instead”**. The panel title becomes
**Host processes (this PC)** and lists PID / Name / Arch / Action with a filter box
(**Filter processes…**). Find `SlopTarget.exe` and attach it.

![Targets panel listing host processes](../screenshots/workspace.png)

The same from an agent:

```json
{ "tool": "target", "action": "list", "params": {} }
{ "tool": "target", "action": "attach", "params": { "pid": 12345 } }
```

`list` returns up to 4096 processes with `pid`, `name`, `arch`, `path` and `elevation`;
filter client-side. `attach` also loads the process's main module into the image session
when nothing is loaded, so the Disassembly tab has something to show
(`image_auto_loaded` in the reply).

## 3. Scan for a value

The **Scanner** panel is the Cheat-Engine flow:

1. Pick a width (`u32`, `f32`, `u64`, …) and a scan kind (`exact`, `between`, `changed`,
   `increased`, `decreased`, …).
2. Type the current value and press **First**.
3. Change the value in the target (`set health 87` in the SlopTarget console, or just let
   `auto` tick), type the new value, press **Next** until a handful of hits remain.
4. Add a hit to the watchlist with the **Add to watchlist** button on its row.

From an agent:

```json
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "scan",
  "params": { "kind": "exact", "width": "u32", "value": 100 } }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "rescan",
  "params": { "kind": "decreased", "width": "u32" } }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "watch_add",
  "params": { "addr": "0x7FF6A1B2C3D4", "width": "u32", "label": "player.health" } }
```

`scan` returns hits with addresses and values; `rescan` narrows the same scan state.
`scan_state` reports whether a scan is live, `scan_reset` clears it.

## 4. Freeze it

The **Watchlist** table has a **Freeze** column. Toggling it makes the watch service write
the captured value back about 10 times a second. `*` next to a value means the entry is
frozen.

```json
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "watch_set",
  "params": { "id": 1, "freeze": true } }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "watch_freeze_once", "params": { "id": 1 } }
{ "tool": "memory", "action": "watch_undo", "params": { "id": 1 } }
```

`watch_freeze_once` releases after the first write-back; `watch_undo` restores the value
captured when the entry was added. The SlopTarget fixture prints
`[!] frozen_probe is N (external freeze detected)` when a freeze is visible from the
target's side — a cheap way to prove the write actually landed.

## 5. Find what writes the address

This is where the local debugger comes in. The four one-shot composite flows
(`ps4_until`, `ps4_find_write`, `ps4_trace_calls`, `ps4_trace_steps`) run on the **local
Win32 debugger** whenever the attached session is a local process — the `ps4_` prefix is
just the historical name, the reply carries `"debugger": "user"`.

```json
{ "tool": "debugger", "action": "ps4_find_write",
  "params": { "addr": "0x7FF6A1B2C3D4", "len": 4, "timeout_ms": 10000 } }
```

The flow: arm a hardware write watchpoint on the address, resume the process, wait for the
trap, then walk the stack of the thread that wrote. The reply contains `halted`, the stop
`event` (registers), `callstack`, `writer_rip` and `writer_rip_hex`. If nothing writes in
time, `halted` is false and the process is left running.

Related one-shots:

| Action | What it does locally |
| --- | --- |
| `ps4_until {addr, timeout_ms}` | run until an address is hit, one-shot breakpoint |
| `ps4_trace_calls {addr, count, timeout_ms}` | log the 6 argument registers at each call to `addr` |
| `ps4_trace_steps {lwpid, count, timeout_ms}` | single-step trace with disassembly per step |
| `ps4_detach` | detach the local debugger (the process keeps running) |

`debugger.status` reports the local debugger as
`local_debugger: { attached, pid, stopped }` alongside the PS4 fields.

The local debugger attaches with `DebugActiveProcess`, so it needs the same access rights
as the backend, and a process that already has a debugger cannot be attached again. It
never kills the target on exit (`DebugSetProcessKillOnExit(FALSE)`).

## What does not work without a console

`ps4_attach`, `ps4_bp_set`, `ps4_watch_set`, `ps4_continue`, `ps4_regs`, `ps4_call`,
`ps4_scan*`, `ps4_turbo_*`, `ps4_dump_module` and the rest of the console surface need a
connected PS4 — they talk to the payload, not to Windows. Static analysis, the decompiler,
the emulator, Lua, the network tools and the scanner/watchlist all work locally.

## 6. Keep going

- [Live memory](../features/live-memory.md) — scan kinds, AOB, pointer chains, snapshots.
- [Live debugging](../features/live-debugging.md) — the console debugger for comparison.
- [Tests](../project/tests.md) — how the fixture and the fake ps4debug server are used in CI.

```

`examples/README.md`:

```md
# Lua examples

Scripts for reverse-slop's Lua 5.4 engine (API reference: the header comment of
`src/core/script/lua_engine.hpp` and the README's "Lua scripting" section).
They run against the same session as the UI: the attached process (PS4 console
or local), the loaded image, renames and comments.

| Script | Needs | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `ps4_find_value.lua` | PS4 with ps4debug-NG | Connects, attaches to a game process, scans for a 32-bit value and narrows the hits while you change the value in-game. |
| `ps4_breakpoint_trace.lua` | PS4 with ps4debug-NG | Sets a software breakpoint, waits for the hit, prints registers and the call stack, then removes the breakpoint and resumes. |
| `ps4_eboot_overview.lua` | a dumped `eboot.bin` / module (ELF) | Loads the image, waits for analysis, lists the largest functions and the code referencing interesting strings. |
| `ue5_dumper.lua` | a process running an Unreal Engine 5.x x64 build (PS4 or PC) | Walks `GObjects`/`GNames` and dumps classes, properties and functions (Dumpspace-style `ClassesInfo.json` + `FNames.txt`). |

## Running

- **Scripts panel**: open the script, edit the `ARGS` table at the top, `Ctrl+Enter`.
- **MCP**: `script` tool, `action=run`, `code=<file contents>`, `timeout_ms` as needed.
  The engine caps a single run (see the `script` tool description); on big games
  lower the dumper's `max_objects` if a run hits the cap.
- **`/api`**: same `script.run` action.

### Parameters

Every example starts with

```lua
ARGS = ARGS or { ... defaults ... }
```

so a caller can prepend its own table instead of editing the file, e.g. over MCP:

```text
code = 'ARGS = { host = "192.168.1.50", process = "eboot.bin", value = 100 }\n' .. <file contents>
```

Unset fields fall back to the defaults shown in each script.

### Sandbox

Scripts run sandboxed by default: no `io`, no `os` (except `os.clock`/`os.time`/
`os.difftime`), no `require`/`package`/`debug`. Results come back through `print()`
and the script's return value. Only `ue5_dumper.lua` writes files, and only when
`ARGS.output_dir` is set **and** the `script_unsafe` setting is enabled
(`app.settings_set {key:"script_unsafe", value:true}` or the Settings dialog);
otherwise it prints the dump instead.

### Addresses

Values like `0x...` are console (or process) virtual addresses. PS4 is x86-64;
game data usually lives above `0x200000000`. Find candidates with the scanner,
`ps4_find_value.lua` or the module list (`target` tool, `action=modules`).

```

`examples/ps4_breakpoint_trace.lua`:

```lua
-- ps4_breakpoint_trace.lua
-- Break once at an address in a PS4 game (ps4debug-NG), dump registers and the
-- call stack of the halted thread, then remove the breakpoint and resume.
-- Typical use: find who writes a value (ps4_find_value.lua), disassemble the
-- writer, then trace its callers with this script.
ARGS = ARGS or {}
local host     = ARGS.host or "192.168.1.50"
local process  = ARGS.process or "eboot.bin"   -- substring of the process name
local addr     = ARGS.addr                     -- breakpoint address (required)
local wait_ms  = ARGS.wait_ms or 30000          -- how long to wait for the hit
local depth    = ARGS.depth or 16              -- call stack frames
if not addr then error("set ARGS.addr to the instruction address to break on") end

local function show(v, indent)
  indent = indent or ""
  if type(v) ~= "table" then return tostring(v) end
  local keys = {}
  for k in pairs(v) do keys[#keys + 1] = k end
  table.sort(keys, function(a, b) return tostring(a) < tostring(b) end)
  local parts = {}
  for _, k in ipairs(keys) do
    local x = v[k]
    if type(x) == "number" and math.type(x) == "integer" and x > 0xFFFF then
      parts[#parts + 1] = string.format("%s%s=0x%X", indent, tostring(k), x)
    elseif type(x) == "table" then
      parts[#parts + 1] = string.format("%s%s={\n%s\n%s}", indent, tostring(k), show(x, indent .. "  "), indent)
    else
      parts[#parts + 1] = string.format("%s%s=%s", indent, tostring(k), tostring(x))
    end
  end
  return table.concat(parts, "\n")
end

-- console, process, debugger
if (slop.target.status().backend or ""):upper() ~= "PS4" then
  print("connecting to " .. host)
  slop.ps4.connect(host)
end
local pid
for _, p in ipairs(slop.target.list()) do
  if p.name and p.name:find(process, 1, true) then pid = p.pid; break end
end
if not pid then error("no process matching '" .. process .. "'") end
slop.debugger.attach(pid)
print(string.format("debugging pid %d, breakpoint at 0x%X", pid, addr))

local bp = slop.debugger.bp_set(addr)
local cleaned = false
local function cleanup()
  if cleaned then return end
  cleaned = true
  pcall(slop.debugger.bp_clear, addr)
  pcall(slop.debugger.continue)
end

local ok, err = pcall(function()
  print("bp: " .. show(bp))
  slop.debugger.continue()
  local stop = slop.debugger.wait(wait_ms)
  if not (stop and stop.halted) then
    print(string.format("no hit within %d ms", wait_ms))
    return
  end
  local lwpid = stop.lwpid or stop.tid
  print("== halted ==\n" .. show(stop))
  print("== registers ==\n" .. show(slop.debugger.regs(lwpid)))
  print("== call stack ==\n" .. show(slop.debugger.callstack(lwpid, depth)))
end)
cleanup()
if not ok then error(err) end
return "done"

```

`examples/ps4_eboot_overview.lua`:

```lua
-- ps4_eboot_overview.lua
-- Static overview of a dumped PS4 module (decrypted eboot.bin / .sprx as ELF,
-- e.g. produced by target.ps4_dump_module): load it into the shared session,
-- wait for analysis, then list the largest functions and the code that
-- references strings matching ARGS.keywords. Renames/comments made afterwards
-- in the UI apply to the same session.
ARGS = ARGS or {}
local path     = ARGS.path                     -- dumped module on the PC (required)
local keywords = ARGS.keywords or { "health", "ammo", "player", "damage", "debug" }
local top_n    = ARGS.top_n or 15
local wait_ms  = ARGS.wait_ms or 120000
local per_key  = ARGS.per_keyword or 5
if not path then error("set ARGS.path to the dumped eboot/module file") end

if not slop.image.load(path) then error("could not load " .. path) end
local st = slop.image.status()
print(string.format("loaded %s base=0x%X entry=0x%X", st.name or path, st.base or 0, st.entry or 0))
if not slop.image.wait_ready(wait_ms) then
  print("analysis still running after " .. wait_ms .. " ms; results below may be partial")
end

-- largest functions: usually the game loop, renderers, big state machines
local fns = slop.disasm.functions(100000)
table.sort(fns, function(a, b) return (a.size or 0) > (b.size or 0) end)
print(string.format("\n== %d largest of %d functions ==", math.min(top_n, #fns), #fns))
for i = 1, math.min(top_n, #fns) do
  local f = fns[i]
  print(string.format("  0x%X  %-32s %6d bytes", f.va, f.name or "?", f.size or 0))
end

-- strings of interest and the functions that use them
local strings = slop.disasm.strings(5, 200000)
print(string.format("\n== %d strings scanned ==", #strings))
for _, key in ipairs(keywords) do
  local shown = 0
  local needle = key:lower()
  for _, s in ipairs(strings) do
    if shown >= per_key then break end
    if s.text and s.text:lower():find(needle, 1, true) then
      local users = {}
      for _, x in ipairs(slop.disasm.xrefs_to(s.va)) do
        local fn = slop.disasm.function_at(x.from)
        users[#users + 1] = fn and string.format("%s+0x%X", fn.name, x.from - fn.va)
                                or string.format("0x%X", x.from)
        if #users >= 4 then break end
      end
      print(string.format("  [%s] 0x%X %q <- %s", key, s.va, s.text:sub(1, 60),
                          #users > 0 and table.concat(users, ", ") or "no code xrefs"))
      shown = shown + 1
    end
  end
end
return #fns

```

`examples/ps4_find_value.lua`:

```lua
-- ps4_find_value.lua
-- Find the address of a 32-bit game value on a PS4 (ps4debug-NG):
--   1. connect to the console and attach to the game process
--   2. exact-scan for ARGS.value
--   3. optionally keep re-reading the hits for ARGS.wait_ms while you change
--      the value in-game, keeping only addresses that now hold ARGS.next_value
-- Returns the surviving addresses (hex) so they can be fed to the watchlist.
ARGS = ARGS or {}
local host       = ARGS.host or "192.168.1.50"   -- console IP
local process    = ARGS.process or "eboot.bin"   -- substring of the process name
local value      = ARGS.value or 100             -- current in-game value
local next_value = ARGS.next_value               -- value after you change it (optional)
local wait_ms    = ARGS.wait_ms or 30000         -- how long to wait for the change
local width      = ARGS.width or "i32"           -- i8..u64, f32, f64
local scan_begin = ARGS.scan_begin               -- optional address range
local scan_end   = ARGS.scan_end
local max_show   = ARGS.max_show or 32

local function fmt_bytes_for(width_name)
  local map = { i8 = "<i1", u8 = "<I1", i16 = "<i2", u16 = "<I2", i32 = "<i4", u32 = "<I4",
                i64 = "<i8", u64 = "<I8", f32 = "<f", f64 = "<d" }
  local f = map[width_name]
  if not f then error("unsupported width " .. tostring(width_name)) end
  return f, string.packsize(f)
end
local unpack_fmt, value_size = fmt_bytes_for(width)

-- 1. console + process
if (slop.target.status().backend or ""):upper() ~= "PS4" then
  print("connecting to " .. host)
  slop.ps4.connect(host)
end
local pid, name
for _, p in ipairs(slop.target.list()) do
  if p.name and p.name:find(process, 1, true) then pid, name = p.pid, p.name; break end
end
if not pid then error("no process matching '" .. process .. "' on the console") end
local ok, attached = slop.target.attach(pid)
if not ok then error("attach to pid " .. pid .. " failed") end
print(string.format("attached to %s (pid %d)", attached or name, pid))

-- 2. first scan
local cfg = { kind = "exact", width = width, value = value, alignment = math.min(value_size, 4) }
if scan_begin then cfg.begin = scan_begin end
if scan_end then cfg["end"] = scan_end end
local hits = slop.mem.scan(cfg)
print(string.format("scan %s == %s: %d hits%s", width, tostring(value), #hits,
                    #hits >= 10000 and " (capped, narrow the range)" or ""))

-- 3. narrow while the value changes in-game
local function read_value(addr)
  local okr, raw = pcall(slop.mem.read_bytes, addr, value_size)
  if not okr or not raw or #raw < value_size then return nil end
  return (string.unpack(unpack_fmt, raw))
end

if next_value ~= nil and #hits > 0 then
  print(string.format("change the value in-game to %s within %d s...", tostring(next_value), wait_ms // 1000))
  local deadline = os.clock() + wait_ms / 1000
  local survivors = hits
  repeat
    local still = {}
    for _, a in ipairs(survivors) do
      local v = read_value(a)
      if v == next_value then still[#still + 1] = a end
    end
    if #still > 0 then survivors = still; break end
  until os.clock() >= deadline
  if survivors == hits then
    print("value never changed to " .. tostring(next_value) .. "; keeping the first-scan hits")
  end
  hits = survivors
  print(string.format("%d address(es) now hold %s", #hits, tostring(next_value)))
end

local out = {}
for i = 1, math.min(#hits, max_show) do
  out[#out + 1] = string.format("0x%X", hits[i])
  print(string.format("  0x%X = %s", hits[i], tostring(read_value(hits[i]))))
end
if #hits > max_show then print(string.format("  ... %d more", #hits - max_show)) end
return table.concat(out, ",")

```

`examples/ue5_dumper.lua`:

```lua
-- ============================================================================
-- ue5_dumper.lua
-- reverse-slop SDK dumper for Unreal Engine 5.x x64 builds (PS4 or PC: both
-- are x86-64, the object layout below is the same for a given engine version).
--
-- Walks FUObjectArray (GObjects) + FNamePool (GNames) of the attached process
-- and emits a Dumpspace-style ClassesInfo.json (classes/structs with their
-- properties and functions) plus FNames.txt.
--
-- Parameters (prepend `ARGS = {...}` or edit the defaults):
--   gobjects    FUObjectArray address (required; find via AOB/xrefs)
--   gnames      FNamePool address (required)
--   output_dir  write files there (needs the script_unsafe setting); when
--               unset or sandboxed the dump is printed instead
--   max_objects hard cap for the object walk (default 400000)
--   verbose     progress every 5000 objects
--   layout      table overriding any offset below, e.g. {UFN_FUNCTIONFLAGS_OFFSET=0xB8}
--
-- Tested layout: UE 5.3.x. Run via the Scripts panel or the `script` MCP tool
-- (action=run) with a large timeout_ms.
-- ============================================================================
ARGS = ARGS or {}
local GObjects_VA = ARGS.gobjects or 0
local GNames_VA   = ARGS.gnames or 0
local OUTPUT_DIR  = ARGS.output_dir
local MAX_OBJECTS = ARGS.max_objects or 400000
local VERBOSE     = ARGS.verbose or false

local L = {}
-- ==== UE 5.x LAYOUT CONSTANTS ==============================================
-- FUObjectArray (UE 5.3.x)
L.UOA_OBJOBJECTS_OFFSET   = 0x10   -- ObjObjects: FChunkedFixedUObjectArray
-- FChunkedFixedUObjectArray
L.CFA_OBJECTS_OFFSET      = 0x00   -- Objects: FUObjectItem**
L.CFA_MAXELEMENTS_OFFSET  = 0x14   -- MaxElements
L.CFA_NUMELEMENTS_OFFSET  = 0x18   -- NumElements
L.CFA_MAXCHUNKS_OFFSET    = 0x1C   -- MaxChunks
L.CFA_NUMCHUNKS_OFFSET    = 0x20   -- NumChunks
L.ELEMENTS_PER_CHUNK      = 64 * 1024 -- 65536
-- FUObjectItem (24 bytes on x64)
L.UOI_SIZE                = 24
L.UOI_OBJECT_OFFSET       = 0x00   -- UObject*
L.UOI_FLAGS_OFFSET        = 0x08
L.UOI_CLUSTER_OFFSET      = 0x0C
L.UOI_SERIAL_OFFSET       = 0x10

-- UObject layout (UE 5.x, no editor)
L.UO_VTABLE_OFFSET        = 0x00
L.UO_OBJECTFLAGS_OFFSET   = 0x08
L.UO_INTERNALINDEX_OFFSET = 0x0C
L.UO_CLASSPRIVATE_OFFSET  = 0x10
L.UO_NAMEPRIVATE_OFFSET   = 0x18   -- FName (8 bytes: ComparisonIndex + Number)
L.UO_OUTERPRIVATE_OFFSET  = 0x20

-- UStruct layout (extends UObject)
L.US_SUPERSTRUCT_OFFSET   = 0x40   -- UStruct*
L.US_CHILDREN_OFFSET      = 0x48   -- UField* (only functions in UE5.3)
L.US_CHILDPROPS_OFFSET    = 0x50   -- FField* (all FProperties)
L.US_PROPERTIES_SIZE_OFF  = 0x58   -- int32 PropertiesSize
L.US_MIN_ALIGN_OFFSET     = 0x5C   -- int32 MinAlignment

-- UFunction extra fields (extends UStruct)
L.UFN_FUNCTIONFLAGS_OFFSET = 0xB0  -- EFunctionFlags (varies by build)

-- FField (UE 5.x FProperty base)
L.FF_VTABLE_OFFSET        = 0x00
L.FF_CLASSPRIVATE_OFFSET  = 0x08   -- FFieldClass*
L.FF_NEXT_OFFSET          = 0x20   -- FField* (linked list of fields)
L.FF_NAMEPRIVATE_OFFSET   = 0x28   -- FName

-- FProperty (extends FField)
L.FP_ARRAYDIM_OFFSET      = 0x38
L.FP_ELEMENTSIZE_OFFSET   = 0x3C
L.FP_OFFSET_OFFSET        = 0x4C   -- int32 Offset_Internal
L.FP_PROPERTYFLAGS_OFFSET = 0x40   -- EPropertyFlags (uint64)

-- FName (UE 5.x): { uint32 ComparisonIndex; uint32 Number; } == 8 bytes
-- FNamePool block resolution:
--   PoolAlignment = 2 (bytes) -> block_index = idx >> 16, byte_offset = (idx & 0xFFFF) * 2
--   Blocks[block_index] + byte_offset -> FNameEntry
-- FNameEntry: uint16 header, then string bytes
--   header layout: bit 0 = bIsWide, next 5 = LowercaseProbeHash, next 10 = Len

-- FNamePool layout (UE 5.3.x default: 0x10 header + blocks array)
L.NP_HEADER_SIZE          = 0x10
L.NP_BLOCKS_OFFSET        = L.NP_HEADER_SIZE
L.NP_STRIDE_SHIFT         = 1     -- entries are 2-byte aligned within a block
L.NP_BLOCK_SIZE_BYTES     = 128 * 1024 -- 128KB per block (2^16 * 2)

for k, v in pairs(ARGS.layout or {}) do
  if L[k] == nil then error("unknown layout key " .. tostring(k)) end
  L[k] = v
end

-- ==== MEMORY HELPERS ========================================================
-- reads that fail (unmapped/freed pages) yield 0 / "" instead of aborting the walk
local function read_raw(addr, len)
  local ok, raw = pcall(slop.mem.read_bytes, addr, len)
  if ok and raw and #raw == len then return raw end
  return nil
end
local function read_u64(addr)
  local raw = read_raw(addr, 8); if not raw then return 0 end
  return (string.unpack("<I8", raw))
end
local function read_u32(addr)
  local raw = read_raw(addr, 4); if not raw then return 0 end
  return (string.unpack("<I4", raw))
end
local function read_u16(addr)
  local raw = read_raw(addr, 2); if not raw then return 0 end
  return (string.unpack("<I2", raw))
end
local function read_cstr(addr, maxlen)
  local raw = read_raw(addr, maxlen or 256); if not raw then return "" end
  return raw:match("^[^%z]*")
end
local function read_wstr(addr, chars)
  local raw = read_raw(addr, chars * 2); if not raw then return "" end
  local out = {}
  for i = 1, #raw - 1, 2 do
    local cp = string.unpack("<I2", raw, i)
    if cp == 0 then break end
    out[#out + 1] = utf8.char(cp)
  end
  return table.concat(out)
end

-- ==== FNAME RESOLUTION ======================================================
local fname_cache = {}
local function fname_string(comparison_index)
  if fname_cache[comparison_index] then return fname_cache[comparison_index] end
  if comparison_index == 0 then return "None" end

  local block_idx = comparison_index >> 16
  local byte_off  = (comparison_index & 0xFFFF) << L.NP_STRIDE_SHIFT
  local block_ptr_va = GNames_VA + L.NP_BLOCKS_OFFSET + block_idx * 8
  local block_base = read_u64(block_ptr_va)
  if block_base == 0 then
    local s = string.format("<bad_block_%d>", block_idx)
    fname_cache[comparison_index] = s
    return s
  end
  local entry_va = block_base + byte_off
  local header = read_u16(entry_va)
  local is_wide = header & 0x1
  local len = header >> 6
  if len == 0 or len > 1024 then
    local s = string.format("<bad_entry_len_%d>", len)
    fname_cache[comparison_index] = s
    return s
  end

  local s
  if is_wide == 0 then
    s = read_cstr(entry_va + 2, len)
  else
    s = read_wstr(entry_va + 2, len)
  end
  fname_cache[comparison_index] = s
  return s
end

local function fname_of(name_priv_va)
  local comp = read_u32(name_priv_va)
  local num  = read_u32(name_priv_va + 4)
  local s = fname_string(comp)
  if num > 0 then return s .. "_" .. tostring(num - 1) end
  return s
end

-- ==== FUOBJECTARRAY WALKER ==================================================
local function get_object_by_index(chunks_ptr, idx)
  local chunk_idx = idx // L.ELEMENTS_PER_CHUNK
  local within    = idx % L.ELEMENTS_PER_CHUNK
  local chunk_ptr = read_u64(chunks_ptr + chunk_idx * 8)
  if chunk_ptr == 0 then return 0 end
  local item_va = chunk_ptr + within * L.UOI_SIZE
  return read_u64(item_va + L.UOI_OBJECT_OFFSET), item_va
end

local function walk_objects()
  local obj_obj_va = GObjects_VA + L.UOA_OBJOBJECTS_OFFSET
  local chunks_ptr = read_u64(obj_obj_va + L.CFA_OBJECTS_OFFSET)
  local num_elems  = read_u32(obj_obj_va + L.CFA_NUMELEMENTS_OFFSET)
  local num_chunks = read_u32(obj_obj_va + L.CFA_NUMCHUNKS_OFFSET)
  print(string.format("[GObjects] Chunks=0x%X NumElems=%d NumChunks=%d",
                       chunks_ptr, num_elems, num_chunks))
  if num_elems > MAX_OBJECTS then num_elems = MAX_OBJECTS end

  local by_index = {}       -- idx -> {va, class_va, name, outer_idx}
  for i = 0, num_elems - 1 do
    local uobj_va = get_object_by_index(chunks_ptr, i)
    if uobj_va ~= 0 then
      local class_va = read_u64(uobj_va + L.UO_CLASSPRIVATE_OFFSET)
      local outer_va = read_u64(uobj_va + L.UO_OUTERPRIVATE_OFFSET)
      local name     = fname_of(uobj_va + L.UO_NAMEPRIVATE_OFFSET)
      by_index[i] = { va=uobj_va, class_va=class_va, outer_va=outer_va, name=name }
    end
    if VERBOSE and i % 5000 == 0 then print("  walked "..i) end
  end
  print("[GObjects] indexed " .. tostring((function()local c=0;for _ in pairs(by_index) do c=c+1 end;return c end)()) .. " live objects")
  return by_index
end

-- ==== FIELD/PROPERTY WALK ==================================================
local function walk_properties(struct_va)
  local props = {}
  local head = read_u64(struct_va + L.US_CHILDPROPS_OFFSET)
  local guard = 0
  while head ~= 0 and guard < 4096 do
    local pname   = fname_of(head + L.FF_NAMEPRIVATE_OFFSET)
    local pclass  = read_u64(head + L.FF_CLASSPRIVATE_OFFSET)  -- FFieldClass*
    local pclass_name_va = pclass ~= 0 and (pclass + 0x00) or 0  -- FFieldClass.Name is at 0
    local ptype = pclass_name_va ~= 0 and fname_of(pclass_name_va) or "<unknown>"
    local poff  = read_u32(head + L.FP_OFFSET_OFFSET)
    local psize = read_u32(head + L.FP_ELEMENTSIZE_OFFSET)
    local pdim  = read_u32(head + L.FP_ARRAYDIM_OFFSET)
    local pflag = read_u64(head + L.FP_PROPERTYFLAGS_OFFSET)
    props[#props+1] = { name=pname, type=ptype, offset=poff, size=psize, dim=pdim, flags=pflag }
    head = read_u64(head + L.FF_NEXT_OFFSET)
    guard = guard + 1
  end
  return props
end

local function walk_functions(struct_va)
  local fns = {}
  local head = read_u64(struct_va + L.US_CHILDREN_OFFSET)
  local guard = 0
  while head ~= 0 and guard < 4096 do
    local fname = fname_of(head + L.UO_NAMEPRIVATE_OFFSET)
    local flags = read_u32(head + L.UFN_FUNCTIONFLAGS_OFFSET)
    local params = walk_properties(head)
    fns[#fns+1] = { name=fname, flags=flags, params=params }
    head = read_u64(head + L.FF_NEXT_OFFSET)
    guard = guard + 1
  end
  return fns
end

-- ==== JSON EMIT =============================================================
local function json_escape(s)
  return (s or ""):gsub("\\", "\\\\"):gsub("\"", "\\\""):gsub("\n", "\\n"):gsub("\r", "\\r")
end
local function json_val(v)
  if type(v) == "string" then return string.format('"%s"', json_escape(v)) end
  if type(v) == "number" then
    if v == math.floor(v) then return string.format("%d", v) end
    return tostring(v)
  end
  if type(v) == "boolean" then return v and "true" or "false" end
  if v == nil then return "null" end
  return tostring(v)
end
local function emit_kv_pairs(t, keys)
  local parts = {}
  for _, k in ipairs(keys) do parts[#parts+1] = string.format('"%s":%s', k, json_val(t[k])) end
  return "{" .. table.concat(parts, ",") .. "}"
end

-- ==== OUTPUT ================================================================
local function classes_json(structs)
  local out = { "[" }
  for i, s in ipairs(structs) do
    local props, fns = {}, {}
    for _, p in ipairs(s.props or {}) do
      props[#props + 1] = "      " .. emit_kv_pairs(p, {"name", "type", "offset", "size", "dim", "flags"})
    end
    for _, fn in ipairs(s.fns or {}) do
      fns[#fns + 1] = "      " .. emit_kv_pairs({name = fn.name, flags = fn.flags}, {"name", "flags"})
    end
    out[#out + 1] = string.format('  {\n    "name": %s,\n    "va": %d,\n    "super": %d,\n' ..
      '    "properties": [\n%s\n    ],\n    "functions": [\n%s\n    ]\n  }%s',
      json_val(s.name), s.va, s.super or 0, table.concat(props, ",\n"), table.concat(fns, ",\n"),
      i < #structs and "," or "")
  end
  out[#out + 1] = "]"
  return table.concat(out, "\n")
end

local function fnames_txt()
  local keys = {}
  for k in pairs(fname_cache) do keys[#keys + 1] = k end
  table.sort(keys)
  local lines = {}
  for _, k in ipairs(keys) do lines[#lines + 1] = string.format("%d\t%s", k, fname_cache[k]) end
  return table.concat(lines, "\n") .. "\n"
end

local function write_file(name, text)
  local path = OUTPUT_DIR .. "\\" .. name
  local f, err = io.open(path, "w")
  if not f then error("cannot write " .. path .. ": " .. tostring(err)) end
  f:write(text)
  f:close()
  print("wrote " .. path)
end

-- ==== DRIVER ================================================================
local function main()
  if GObjects_VA == 0 or GNames_VA == 0 then
    error("set ARGS.gobjects and ARGS.gnames (FUObjectArray / FNamePool addresses)")
  end
  if OUTPUT_DIR and io == nil then
    print("output_dir ignored: file output needs the script_unsafe setting; printing the dump instead")
    OUTPUT_DIR = nil
  end

  local start = os.clock()
  local objects = walk_objects()
  print(string.format("walked in %.1fs", os.clock() - start))

  -- classify: which objects are UStructs (classes/structs), enums, functions
  local structs, enums, functions = {}, {}, {}
  for _, info in pairs(objects) do
    if info.class_va and info.class_va ~= 0 then
      local cls = objects[read_u32(info.class_va + L.UO_INTERNALINDEX_OFFSET)]
      local cname = cls and cls.name or "?"
      if cname == "Class" or cname == "ScriptStruct" then
        info.props = walk_properties(info.va)
        info.fns   = walk_functions(info.va)
        info.super = read_u64(info.va + L.US_SUPERSTRUCT_OFFSET)
        structs[#structs + 1] = info
      elseif cname == "Enum" then
        enums[#enums + 1] = info
      elseif cname == "Function" then
        functions[#functions + 1] = info
      end
    end
  end
  table.sort(structs, function(a, b) return a.name < b.name end)
  print(string.format("classified: %d struct-like, %d enums, %d functions",
                      #structs, #enums, #functions))

  local classes = classes_json(structs)
  if OUTPUT_DIR then
    write_file("ClassesInfo.json", classes)
    write_file("FNames.txt", fnames_txt())
  else
    print("== ClassesInfo.json ==")
    print(classes)
  end
  return string.format("%d classes/structs, %d enums, %d functions", #structs, #enums, #functions)
end

return main()

```

`integrations/ps4-mcp-adapters/README.md`:

```md
# PS4-MCP analyzer adapters (ported into PS4-Slop)

The IDA / Ghidra / Binary Ninja / iaito adapters from PS4-MCP, rewired to
PS4-Slop's **built-in MCP server** instead of the Rust broker's custom `/rpc`
protocol.

```
integrations/ps4-mcp-adapters/
├── ps4_mcp/                  adapter package (from PS4-MCP, unchanged logic)
│   ├── client.py             NEW: BrokerClient shim speaking MCP JSON-RPC to
│   │                         http://127.0.0.1:8765/mcp (PS4-Slop's server)
│   ├── config.py             validation helpers (verbatim)
│   ├── agents.py             analyzer-side analysis worker (verbatim)
│   └── adapters/             base/ida/ghidra/binja/iaito (verbatim)
└── scripts/
    ├── ida/ps4_connect.py        run inside IDA's Python
    ├── ghidra/ps4_connect.py     Ghidra script (Python); PS4Mcp.java +
    │                             ApplyWorkbenchAnnotation.java are the upstream
    │                             Java plugin — they still target the PS4-MCP
    │                             /rpc broker and are kept for reference
    ├── binja/ps4_connect.py      run inside Binary Ninja's Python
    ├── iaito/ps4_connect.py      run with r2/iaito (r2pipe)
    └── live/start-live.ps1       start the engine + GDB-RSP bridge
```

## Wiring

PS4-Slop's engine already serves MCP on `127.0.0.1:8765` (`POST /mcp`,
JSON-RPC 2.0). The shim in `ps4_mcp/client.py` keeps the `BrokerClient`
interface the adapters were written against and maps the broker operations
onto PS4-Slop tools:

| PS4-MCP broker op   | PS4-Slop MCP tool.action | Notes |
| ------------------- | ------------------------ | ----- |
| `state`             | `target.status`          | synthesized broker-state view |
| `events`            | `debugger.ps4_events`    | console stop-event drain |
| `release`           | local no-op              |       |
| `memory_peek`       | `memory.read`            | live console read, hex out |
| `process_maps`      | `target.regions` (+`modules` for names) | `start/end/name/protection` shape |
| `ftp_download`      | `target.ps4_dump_module` | dumps a module over ps4debug-NG to a local file, sha256 reported |
| `payload_execute`   | `debugger.ps4_elf_load`  | homebrew ELF payload; client-side sha256 verified first |
| `agent_register/poll/result/unregister` | local no-ops | PS4-Slop runs analysis agents through its own MCP loop; `agent_poll` returns `None` |

Environment for the connect scripts: `PS4_SLOP_URL` (default
`http://127.0.0.1:8765`), `PS4_SLOP_ROOT` (adapter root, default is this
checkout). No broker token is needed — PS4-Slop's MCP server is loopback-only
by default; the shim sends `Authorization` only if a token file is passed.

## Console + live debugging

1. Start the engine: `tools/build.ps1 -NoFrontend` then run
   `build/src/engine/reverse-slop-engine.exe` (or just the app).
2. Attach the console from the UI, or via MCP: `target.ps4_connect {host,
   port=744, pid}` / `target.ps4_auto {host}` then `debugger.ps4_attach {pid}`.
3. Open the GDB Remote bridge so an external GDB/LLDB can share the session:
   `gdb` tool `start` (loopback only, `allow_writes` opt-in), then
   `gdb -ex 'target remote 127.0.0.1:2331'`. The UI, MCP agents and the GDB
   client serialize on one console connection through the session broker
   (`src/core/runtime/broker.*`).

## Scope

Only dev-tooling surface was ported. PS4-MCP's game-project authoring
(`games.rs` and friends) and anything cheat-oriented stays out, per
`docs/MERGE.md`.
